questions.title: Async Apex Governor Limits at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: An enterprise org chains Queueable jobs to process a nightly reconciliation against an external system, and also fires Platform Events on the same records. Walk through the specific async limits that collide here — the 50 queued-jobs-per-transaction ceiling, the daily async Apex executions limit, and Platform Event daily delivery limits — and how you'd redesign the job chain so it survives a volume spike without silently dropping work.
questions.modelAnswer: Queueable chaining is capped at 50 jobs enqueued from within an executing Queueable context (unlimited depth of chaining is allowed, but each queueable can only enqueue one more from inside itself in practice, and the org-wide concurrent Apex limit and the 250,000-per-24-hours async Apex method executions ceiling both still apply across the whole org, not just this job). The real risk at enterprise scale isn't the chain depth, it's that a volume spike pushes you toward the daily async executions limit shared by Queueable, Batch, Future, and Scheduled Apex across every other process in the org, so this reconciliation job can starve other automation or get throttled itself. Platform Events add a second ceiling: a High Volume event has its own daily published-events allocation tied to org edition, and because EventBus.publish happens synchronously inside the same transaction as the Queueable's DML, a burst of records can hit that limit before the chain even finishes processing. The redesign is to decouple volume from chain depth: batch the reconciliation through Batch Apex instead of deep Queueable chaining (Batch Apex's own governor limits reset per batch execution context rather than accumulating against the daily async ceiling the same way), publish Platform Events in bulk via a single EventBus.publish call per batch of up to 2,000 events rather than one per record, and add a persisted retry/backlog table so a day that hits the ceiling defers the remainder to the next run instead of silently failing. I'd also instrument daily async usage against org limits proactively (via the Apex Limits API or Event Monitoring) so the team sees the ceiling approaching before a volume spike actually hits it in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by separating two different problems that look like one: how deep my Queueable chain can go, and how much async capacity the whole org has in a day. The 50-enqueue ceiling per transaction almost never bites you in a simple chain, but the daily async executions limit is shared across every Batch, Future, Queueable, and Scheduled job in the org, so a volume spike on this one reconciliation can quietly starve something unrelated. I'd move the heavy lifting into Batch Apex instead of a long Queueable chain, because batch execution contexts don't accumulate against that daily ceiling the same way deep chaining does, and I'd publish Platform Events in bulk, one EventBus.publish call per batch of records, not one call per record, because that's a second limit — the daily published-events allocation — that a burst can hit independently. And the piece I wouldn't skip is a backlog table: if a day does hit a ceiling, I want the leftover work saved and picked up tomorrow, not silently dropped, which is exactly the kind of failure that doesn't show up until someone downstream asks why reconciliation has been wrong for three days.
commonMistakes: Assumes the 50-job chain limit is the binding constraint instead of the shared daily async executions ceiling
Publishes Platform Events one record at a time instead of bulk EventBus.publish calls
Doesn't account for other org automation competing for the same daily async allocation
Has no backlog/retry mechanism, so a limit breach means silently dropped work
Conflates Batch Apex's per-batch governor reset with the org-wide daily async ceiling
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes the per-transaction chain limit from the org-wide daily async executions ceiling
Identifies Platform Event daily publish limits as a separate, independent constraint
Proposes batching and bulk event publishing instead of per-record async calls
Builds in a persisted backlog/retry mechanism for days that hit a ceiling
Recommends proactive monitoring of async/event usage against org limits

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the relevant async and event governor limits
Identifies the real enterprise-scale risk (shared daily ceiling, not chain depth)
Proposes a concrete redesign (batching, bulk publish, backlog)
Includes proactive monitoring of limit usage

questions.title: When Apex Enterprise Patterns (Domain/Service/Selector) Are Worth the Overhead
questions.prompt: A development team is debating adopting a full fflib-style Apex Enterprise Patterns layering — Selector, Domain, Service — for a new org versus just writing straightforward triggers calling handler classes. As the architect, how do you decide, and what do you tell them about the real cost of getting it wrong in either direction?
questions.modelAnswer: The layered pattern earns its cost when an org has enough business complexity that the same logic needs to be reused across multiple entry points — triggers, invocable Apex called from Flow, REST endpoints, batch jobs — and when the team is large enough that strict separation of query logic (Selector), record-level business rules (Domain), and cross-object orchestration (Service) actually prevents collisions rather than just adding ceremony. The failure mode in one direction is skipping the pattern on a genuinely complex org: logic gets duplicated across a trigger handler, an invocable class, and a batch job, so a single business rule change means hunting down three divergent copies, and SOQL queries get scattered everywhere instead of centralized where field-level security and sharing enforcement can be applied consistently. The failure mode in the other direction is over-applying the pattern on a small, simple org or a single isolated feature: three extra classes and multiple layers of indirection for a one-object, one-rule use case slows every developer down and makes a two-line fix a four-file change, which actively hurts an org that will stay small. My actual decision criterion is reuse surface area and team size, not control for its own sake: if this logic will genuinely be called from more than one entry point, or more than two or three developers will touch this domain over its life, the layering pays for itself; if it's a single trigger on a single object with one team maintaining it, a straightforward trigger-to-handler-class pattern with centralized bulkification is enough, and I'd rather ship that than force fflib onto a problem that doesn't need it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them this isn't a style preference, it's a bet about how much this logic is going to get reused and how many hands are going to touch it. If I know this business logic is going to get called from a trigger, an invocable action in Flow, and probably a REST endpoint eventually, I want it in a Service layer once, with Selector classes owning the queries, because otherwise I'm going to have three slightly different copies of the same rule within a year and nobody's going to remember which one is authoritative. But if this is one object, one straightforward rule, and it's going to stay that way, I'm not going to make someone edit four files to fix a typo in a validation message — that's ceremony without a payoff. So my actual question to the team isn't 'is this the proper pattern,' it's 'how many entry points and how many developers is this logic going to see over its life,' and I let that answer, not a style guide, decide.
commonMistakes: Treats Apex Enterprise Patterns as a universal best practice rather than a cost/benefit decision
Applies full layering to a single-object, single-entry-point feature, adding unnecessary ceremony
Skips layering on genuinely complex, multi-entry-point logic, leading to duplicated business rules
Doesn't name reuse surface area or team size as the actual decision criteria
Ignores the ongoing cost to every future developer who has to navigate extra layers for simple changes
keyPoints: Identifies reuse across multiple entry points as the key factor favoring the layered pattern
Identifies team size/longevity as a second factor favoring stricter layering
Names the real cost of over-applying the pattern to simple, isolated logic
Names the real cost of under-applying the pattern to complex, multi-entry-point logic
Gives a concrete, criterion-based decision rule rather than a blanket preference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Names concrete criteria (reuse surface, team size) for the decision
Explains the real cost of over-applying the pattern
Explains the real cost of under-applying the pattern
Provides a clear, defensible decision rule

questions.title: Platform Events vs. Change Data Capture vs. Pub/Sub API
questions.prompt: Explain the actual technical differences between Platform Events, Change Data Capture, and the Pub/Sub API, and describe a concrete enterprise scenario where each one, specifically, is the correct choice over the other two.
questions.modelAnswer: Platform Events are custom-defined event messages you publish deliberately from Apex, Flow, or an external system via the REST/SOAP API, carrying a payload you design yourself — they're the right choice when the event is a business event that doesn't map to a simple record change, like 'ShipmentDelayed__e' carrying a reason code and carrier that isn't just a before/after diff of a record. Change Data Capture automatically publishes change events for standard or custom objects you enable, with a payload that's the actual field-level delta (old and new values) generated by the platform itself with no Apex required to detect or publish it — it's the right choice when the requirement is literally 'tell downstream systems whenever this object's records are created, updated, deleted, or undeleted,' such as keeping an external data warehouse or search index in sync, because you get guaranteed, ordered delivery of every DML without writing and maintaining publish logic yourself. The Pub/Sub API is the modern, gRPC-based streaming interface that both Platform Events and CDC events flow through when the consumer is an external system; it replaced the CometD-based Streaming API as the way external subscribers consume these events with better throughput, schema definitions via Avro, and support for both the event bus channels, so it's not a third type of event, it's the transport layer you choose for how an external subscriber reads either Platform Events or CDC events at scale instead of CometD. A concrete scenario: use CDC to stream every Account and Opportunity change into a Snowflake replica for reporting (no custom publish logic, guaranteed completeness); use a custom Platform Event like LargeDealApproved__e to notify a Slack/ServiceNow integration only when a specific business condition is met, which isn't a raw field diff; and use the Pub/Sub API as the subscriber-side mechanism an external Kafka-based integration layer uses to consume both of those streams reliably with replay support, instead of maintaining a brittle CometD long-polling client.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it by what triggers the event, not by the word 'event' itself, because that's where people get confused. Change Data Capture is automatic — I turn it on for an object and the platform itself emits the before-and-after diff every time a record changes, no Apex involved, so it's my first choice for 'just keep this external system in sync with every change,' like streaming Account and Opportunity changes into a Snowflake replica. A Platform Event is something I define and publish on purpose, with my own payload, for an actual business moment that isn't just a field diff — a shipment got delayed and I want to say why and which carrier, that's not something CDC gives me for free. And the Pub/Sub API isn't a third kind of event at all, it's just the modern streaming transport — it's gRPC-based, it replaced the old CometD Streaming API, and it's how an external system actually subscribes to either of the first two at scale, with replay if it falls behind. So in a real integration I'd typically use all three together: CDC for the raw sync, custom Platform Events for business moments, and Pub/Sub API as how my external Kafka layer actually consumes both.
commonMistakes: Treats Pub/Sub API as a third category of event rather than the transport/subscription layer
Uses a custom Platform Event to replicate a simple field-level change CDC would give for free
Doesn't know CDC payloads include old and new field values automatically with no Apex required
Confuses CometD Streaming API with Pub/Sub API as if they're interchangeable with no tradeoff
Can't name a concrete scenario where each of the three is specifically the right choice
keyPoints: Correctly explains CDC as automatic, platform-generated field-level change events
Correctly explains Platform Events as custom, deliberately published business events
Correctly explains Pub/Sub API as the modern streaming transport/subscription layer, not a third event type
Gives a concrete, differentiated scenario for each of the three
Explains why Pub/Sub API replaced CometD Streaming API for external subscribers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes CDC, Platform Events, and Pub/Sub API technically
Gives concrete, differentiated scenarios for each
Correctly frames Pub/Sub API as transport, not a third event category

questions.title: Salesforce DX Source-Driven Development: Unlocked Packages, 2GP, and Unmanaged Source
questions.prompt: An enterprise org with 12 development teams is moving from change-set-based deployment to a source-driven Salesforce DX model. Explain the real differences between unlocked packages (2GP), org-dependent unlocked packages, and plain unmanaged source-tracked development, and recommend which combination this org should actually use and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Second-generation (2GP) unlocked packages are self-contained, versioned metadata bundles with their own dependency graph and namespace isolation that can be validated and promoted independently, installed into any org without requiring that org to already have specific base metadata present — they're the right fit for a genuinely modular capability (a shared utility library, a specific business domain's objects and Apex) owned end-to-end by one team, because the package boundary forces real separation of concerns and lets that team release on its own cadence without waiting on the other eleven. Org-dependent unlocked packages relax that isolation: they can reference metadata that lives outside the package in the target org (like a field on a standard object another team owns), which makes them easier to adopt incrementally from a messy existing org, but they reintroduce coupling to whatever exists in the destination org, so a given version can succeed in one org and fail in another depending on what's already there — they're a reasonable bridge during migration, not a long-term end state for genuinely independent teams. Plain unmanaged, source-tracked development with no packaging at all is the simplest model and is fine for a single team's straightforward, non-reusable configuration, but at 12 teams it creates exactly the deployment-dependency-ordering chaos change sets already caused, just with better diffing. For this org, I'd recommend defining real package boundaries around actual business domains (not one package per team by org-chart, which just relocates the coupling problem), using real 2GP unlocked packages for anything with a clean ownership boundary and real reuse value, allowing org-dependent packages only as a time-boxed transitional step for the messiest existing shared objects, and keeping a single small unpackaged layer for genuinely org-wide, cross-cutting configuration that doesn't belong to any one domain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on the instinct to just create twelve packages, one per team, because that's org-chart-driven packaging, and it just moves the coupling problem around instead of solving it. Real 2GP unlocked packages are the gold standard here — self-contained, independently versioned, no hidden dependency on what else happens to exist in the target org — and they're worth the setup cost for anything that's a genuine, reusable business domain with one clear owner. Org-dependent unlocked packages I'd treat as a bridge, not a destination: they let you reference metadata outside the package, which is exactly what makes migrating a messy existing org easier in the short term, but that same flexibility means a package version that works in one org can break in another, so I wouldn't want that to be the permanent architecture for twelve independent teams. And plain unmanaged source without any packaging at all, I'd only keep for the genuinely cross-cutting, nobody-owns-this-alone configuration — everything else gets a real package boundary drawn around an actual business capability, not a team name.
commonMistakes: Creates one package per team by org-chart instead of by real business domain boundaries
Treats org-dependent unlocked packages as a permanent architecture rather than a transitional bridge
Doesn't explain that org-dependent packages can succeed in one org and fail in another
Assumes unmanaged source tracking alone solves the 12-team dependency-ordering problem
Confuses namespace isolation in 2GP with simple folder/metadata organization
keyPoints: Correctly explains 2GP unlocked packages' self-contained, namespace-isolated nature
Correctly explains why org-dependent packages reintroduce target-org coupling
Recommends domain-based, not team-based, package boundaries
Positions org-dependent packages as a time-boxed migration bridge, not an end state
Keeps a minimal unpackaged layer only for genuinely cross-cutting configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the technical differences between the three approaches
Recommends domain-based rather than team-based package boundaries
Correctly scopes org-dependent packages as transitional, not permanent

questions.title: Designing a CI/CD Pipeline with Real Deployment Gates
questions.prompt: Design a CI/CD pipeline for Salesforce releases that actually prevents bad code from reaching production, not just automates the deployment mechanics. What gates does it need, in what order, and what happens when one fails?
questions.modelAnswer: A real pipeline runs in stages that get progressively more expensive and catch progressively deeper problems, failing fast on the cheap checks: first, static analysis (PMD for Apex, ESLint for LWC) and a secrets/credential scan on every commit, which catches style and obvious security issues in seconds; second, a scratch-org spin-up that deploys the changed metadata plus its dependencies and runs Apex unit tests with the org-required 75% coverage floor enforced as a hard gate, not a suggestion, plus any LWC Jest tests; third, a deployment validation (checkOnly) against a full-copy or partial-copy sandbox that mirrors production configuration, catching issues that only surface with real data volume or real permission sets that an empty scratch org wouldn't show; and fourth, for anything touching a regulated or high-risk area, a manual review/approval gate before the pipeline is allowed to promote to the next environment. Each gate's failure stops the pipeline entirely rather than letting it proceed with a warning — a failed static analysis check or a coverage drop below the floor should block the merge, not just annotate it, because a gate anyone can route around isn't a gate. The pipeline should also carry a rollback plan as a first-class artifact, not an afterthought: every production deployment should have a corresponding, tested destructive/rollback package or a documented manual rollback procedure attached to the release ticket before it's eligible to deploy, and the pipeline should track deployment metadata (what changed, who approved it, test results) so an incident response doesn't start with someone manually reconstructing what actually shipped. Finally, I'd gate merges to the main release branch with required status checks in source control itself, so the gates are enforced by the platform, not by social convention that an under-deadline engineer can skip.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I care about most isn't automating the deploy step, it's making sure a bad change physically cannot reach production without someone actively overriding a gate, and that override is logged. So I order the checks cheapest-and-fastest first: static analysis and a secrets scan on every commit, because that catches the most common mistakes in seconds and shouldn't need a scratch org spun up to catch a lint error. Then a real scratch org build plus unit tests with coverage enforced as a hard floor — if coverage drops, the pipeline stops, it doesn't just flag it and move on. Then a validation deploy against a sandbox that actually looks like production, because that's where you catch the stuff an empty scratch org can't show you. And for anything touching something regulated or high-risk, I want an actual human to approve before it goes further, not a rubber-stamp automated gate. The piece people skip that I won't is the rollback plan — every release needs one attached before it's even eligible to deploy, because figuring out how to undo a bad release at 2am while production is down is not when you want to be writing that plan for the first time.
commonMistakes: Treats CI/CD as deployment automation only, with no real quality or security gates
Makes test coverage a soft warning instead of a hard, blocking gate
Skips validation against a realistic sandbox, relying only on empty scratch-org tests
Has no rollback plan prepared before a production deployment is allowed to proceed
Enforces gates by convention/documentation rather than by platform-enforced required checks

Treats test coverage and static analysis as hard blocking gates, not warnings
Includes a realistic sandbox validation step beyond scratch-org unit tests
Requires manual approval for high-risk/regulated changes
Requires a tested rollback plan as a precondition for production deployment
Enforces gates via platform-level required checks, not social convention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent, ordered set of real quality/security gates

Enforces gates structurally rather than by convention

questions.title: Shield Platform Encryption: Deterministic vs. Probabilistic, and What Breaks
questions.prompt: A regulated client wants to encrypt SSNs and account balances at rest using Shield Platform Encryption. Explain the real difference between deterministic and probabilistic encryption schemes, and what specifically breaks in reports, list views, and formulas depending on which one you pick.
questions.modelAnswer: Probabilistic encryption produces a different ciphertext every time the same plaintext value is encrypted, which gives the strongest security guarantee because repeated values aren't distinguishable in storage, but it also means the field can't be used in a WHERE clause filter, can't be used in a formula, can't support exact-match or sort operations in a list view, and loses most standard report filtering because the platform can't compare encrypted values to a filter criterion without decrypting every row first. Deterministic encryption produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext every time, which restores the ability to filter on exact match and to sort, and supports a narrower set of formula and validation rule operations, but it leaks pattern information — if two records share the same encrypted SSN, that equality is visible in the ciphertext even without decrypting it, which is a real security tradeoff a compliance team needs to consciously accept, not something that should be a default choice made for developer convenience. For an SSN field specifically, I'd lean deterministic only if there's a genuine business requirement to filter or dedupe on it exactly, and I'd pair that decision with field-level and object-level security plus restricted Apex access, because deterministic encryption alone isn't sufficient protection against pattern-based inference attacks on its own. For account balances, which are typically used in roll-up summaries, formulas, and numeric reports, I'd flag upfront that most numeric aggregation and formula use cases are fundamentally incompatible with either encryption scheme at the field level — roll-up summaries, most report aggregate functions, and many standard formula operators don't work on encrypted fields at all, so the architecture decision here is really about whether the compliance requirement can be satisfied by encrypting a narrower set of truly sensitive fields while leaving aggregatable numeric fields unencrypted and relying on field-level security, or whether the business accepts losing native aggregation on that data entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest first thing I'd tell the client is that encryption and reporting are in tension, and picking between deterministic and probabilistic is really picking which half of that tension you're willing to live with. Probabilistic is the stronger guarantee — same input, different ciphertext every time — but you lose filtering, sorting, and formula support on that field almost completely. Deterministic gets you exact-match filtering and sorting back because the same input always encrypts to the same output, but that consistency is itself a small leak — if two SSNs are identical, you can tell that from the ciphertext pattern alone, so I wouldn't present that as a free lunch, I'd present it as a conscious tradeoff the compliance officer needs to sign off on, not something I pick for them. And for account balances specifically, I'd be upfront that roll-up summaries and most report aggregations just don't work on an encrypted numeric field at all, full stop — so the real conversation isn't 'which encryption mode,' it's 'which fields actually need field-level encryption versus which ones you protect with strict field-level security and leave aggregatable.'
commonMistakes: Treats deterministic encryption as a strictly better default without disclosing the pattern-leak tradeoff
Doesn't realize roll-up summaries and most report aggregations fail on encrypted fields regardless of mode
Assumes probabilistic encryption fields can still be filtered or sorted in list views
Makes the encryption-mode choice unilaterally instead of as a compliance-owned risk decision
Encrypts every sensitive-looking field by default without considering the reporting/aggregation cost
keyPoints: Correctly explains probabilistic encryption's stronger security but loss of filter/sort/formula support
Correctly explains deterministic encryption's exact-match support and its pattern-leak tradeoff
Identifies that roll-up summaries and most aggregate reporting break on encrypted numeric fields
Frames the encryption-mode choice as a compliance decision, not a developer default
Proposes a narrower encryption scope plus field-level security as an alternative to blanket encryption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the deterministic vs. probabilistic technical difference
Correctly identifies what breaks in reports/list views/formulas for each mode
