questions.title: OAuth 2.0 Flows for Salesforce Integration: Choosing the Right One
questions.prompt: An enterprise integration landscape needs to connect Salesforce to: a nightly unattended ETL job, a mobile field-service app used by employees, and a partner's server-to-server API. Explain which OAuth 2.0 flow fits each scenario and why the others would be wrong or risky choices.
questions.modelAnswer: The nightly unattended ETL job should use the JWT Bearer flow: it authenticates as a pre-authorized connected app using a digitally signed JWT and a certificate, with no user present and no stored password or refresh token that could leak, which is exactly the profile of a server process that runs on a schedule with nobody available to approve a login prompt. The mobile field-service app used by employees should use the User-Agent flow or, more robustly, the Authorization Code flow with PKCE, because a real human is present to authenticate interactively, and PKCE specifically protects against the authorization code being intercepted on a mobile device where a traditional client secret can't be stored securely; using the client credentials or JWT flow here would be wrong because those assume no interactive user, and you'd lose per-user context, audit trail, and the ability to apply user-specific permissions and sharing rules. The partner's server-to-server API integration should use the Client Credentials flow (or JWT Bearer with a named integration user, depending on whether per-partner user identity matters) because it's machine-to-machine with no human in the loop on either side, and Client Credentials grants access scoped to a specific integration user's permissions without requiring an interactive consent screen on every token refresh. The flow that's wrong for all three unattended/machine scenarios is the standard Authorization Code flow without PKCE used interactively with a stored refresh token sitting in a config file, because that pattern — common in legacy integrations — creates a long-lived credential that, if it leaks, grants ongoing access with no interactive re-authentication ever required, which is a much larger blast radius than a JWT signed with a certificate that can be rotated and scoped to one connected app.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd match each one to whether there's a real person present, because that's really the whole decision. The nightly ETL job has nobody there to click 'allow,' so it needs JWT Bearer — it's signed with a certificate, there's no password or long-lived secret sitting in a config file that could leak, and it's built specifically for unattended server processes. The mobile app has an actual employee logging in, so I want Authorization Code with PKCE — PKCE specifically protects the authorization code on a mobile client where I can't safely embed a traditional secret, and I still get per-user context and sharing enforcement, which JWT or client credentials would throw away. The partner server-to-server integration is machine-to-machine on both ends, so Client Credentials fits — it's scoped to one integration user, no interactive consent needed on every refresh. What I'd actively flag as a red flag in an existing integration landscape is a stored refresh token sitting in a plaintext config somewhere for an unattended job — that's the classic shortcut that works fine until it leaks, and then you've got a long-lived credential with no easy way to know it's even been compromised.
commonMistakes: Uses a stored refresh token for unattended server jobs instead of JWT Bearer or Client Credentials
Uses Client Credentials or JWT Bearer for an interactive user-facing mobile app, losing per-user context
Doesn't know PKCE exists specifically to protect mobile/public clients that can't store a secret safely
Can't explain why a long-lived stored refresh token is a larger security risk than a signed, rotatable JWT
Picks a single flow for all three scenarios instead of matching the flow to whether a user is present
keyPoints: Correctly recommends JWT Bearer for the unattended server job
Correctly recommends Authorization Code with PKCE for the interactive mobile app
Correctly recommends Client Credentials for the server-to-server partner integration
Explains why each wrong flow would be risky or lose necessary context
Flags stored long-lived refresh tokens as a real security anti-pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches each scenario to the right OAuth flow
Explains why alternative flows would be wrong for each scenario
Identifies the stored-refresh-token anti-pattern as a real risk

questions.title: Advanced SOQL Optimization: Selectivity, Indexes, and the Query Plan Tool
questions.prompt: A custom object with 8 million rows has a SOQL query that times out intermittently in production but runs fine in a sandbox with 50,000 rows. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether the query is actually selective, what the Query Plan tool tells you, and what you'd change.
questions.code: SELECT Id, Name, Status__c FROM Big_Object__c WHERE Status__c = 'Active' AND Region__c = 'EMEA' ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC
questions.modelAnswer: A query that behaves fine at 50,000 rows and times out at 8 million is almost always a selectivity problem that volume exposed rather than created — the optimizer's selectivity threshold (roughly 10% of the first million rows, or a smaller percentage above that, plus a hard cap) means a filter that was 'selective enough' against a small sandbox dataset can fall below the threshold against production volume and get the query planner to fall back to a full table scan. The Query Plan tool in the Developer Console shows the actual access path chosen, the estimated cost, and the cardinality, and critically shows whether an index was actually used — if Status__c alone isn't selective (Active might be 60% of 8 million rows), I'd expect the plan to show a table scan or a much higher relative cost than a plan using a genuinely selective filter. The fix usually isn't adding more filters to the WHERE clause blindly; it's checking whether a standard index exists on the filtered fields (certain fields are indexed automatically — Id, Name, CreatedDate, Lookup/Master-Detail fields, and externalId/unique fields) and, if not, requesting a custom index from Salesforce Support on a field with genuinely high cardinality and selectivity, or restructuring the filter to lead with the most selective condition the platform can actually use. For a field like Status__c with low cardinality, combining it with a genuinely selective secondary filter (like a date range window instead of ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC across the whole table) often gets the compound filter under the selectivity threshold even when neither filter alone would qualify. If the use case is inherently a non-selective, broad query (an 'export all Active records' type requirement), that's a case for Batch Apex with a custom QueryLocator or Bulk API rather than trying to force a synchronous SOQL query to behave like a selective lookup it fundamentally isn't.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that it's fine in a sandbox at 50,000 rows and breaks at 8 million is the tell — that's not a logic bug, that's the query crossing a selectivity threshold that only matters at real volume. First thing I'd do is pull up the Query Plan tool in the Developer Console and actually look at whether it says an index got used, because that's the difference between a fast, narrow index scan and the planner falling back to a full table scan across 8 million rows. If Status__c equals Active covers most of the table, that filter alone was never selective, it just didn't matter at 50,000 rows where even a table scan is fast. So I'd either get a compound filter that's actually selective together — maybe pairing it with a tighter date window instead of sorting the whole table by CreatedDate — or I'd request a custom index from Salesforce Support if there's a genuinely high-cardinality field this needs to filter on regularly. And if what the business actually wants is 'give me every Active EMEA record,' that's not a query I should be forcing through a synchronous SOQL call at all — that's a Batch Apex job with its own QueryLocator, built for exactly this volume.
commonMistakes: Assumes a query that works in a small sandbox will scale linearly to production volume
Doesn't check the Query Plan tool to confirm whether an index was actually used
Adds more WHERE clause filters without checking whether any of them are individually or jointly selective
Tries to force an inherently non-selective, broad query through synchronous SOQL instead of Batch Apex
Doesn't know which fields are indexed by default versus requiring a custom index request
keyPoints: Identifies the selectivity threshold crossing as the real cause, not a sandbox/production bug
Uses the Query Plan tool to confirm index usage and estimated cost/cardinality
Knows which fields are indexed by default and when a custom index request is appropriate
Proposes a genuinely selective compound filter rather than arbitrary added conditions
Recognizes when the use case calls for Batch Apex/Bulk API instead of a synchronous selective query

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the selectivity-threshold root cause
Correctly describes how to use the Query Plan tool to confirm it
Proposes a concrete, technically sound fix (indexing, compound filter)
Recognizes when the right fix is a different execution model (Batch/Bulk)

questions.title: SOSL vs. SOQL at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: A global search feature needs to let service agents find a customer by name, phone, email, or account number across five different objects simultaneously. Explain why SOSL is the architecturally correct choice here over five parallel SOQL queries, and what its real limitations are at enterprise scale.
questions.modelAnswer: SOSL searches the Salesforce search index rather than querying table rows directly, and it can search multiple objects and multiple fields in a single call, which is exactly the shape of a cross-object, fuzzy, multi-field lookup — five parallel SOQL queries would each need their own LIKE-based text matching, would each count separately against the 100-synchronous-SOQL-queries-per-transaction limit, and LIKE '%value%' pattern matching on a non-indexed text field forces a full scan per object rather than using the maintained search index, which gets dramatically worse as each object's row count grows. SOSL's real limitations at enterprise scale start with its 2,000-row return cap across all objects searched in a single SOSL query, which means a very common search term (common last name, common area-code-only phone fragment) can return a capped, effectively arbitrary subset rather than a complete result set, so the UI needs to communicate 'top matches' rather than implying completeness. SOSL also depends on the search index being current — by default there's a near-real-time but not instant indexing delay, so a record created or updated in the last few seconds might not yet be searchable, which matters for a service agent workflow where an agent might be searching for a customer record created moments earlier in the same interaction. Architecturally, I'd pair SOSL for the broad multi-object lookup with a deliberate design decision about which fields are actually searchable (restricting to indexed, genuinely useful match fields rather than searching every text field on every object, which both slows the search and increases noisy matches), and I'd set expectations with the business that this is a 'find candidates fast' tool, with a precise SOQL lookup available as a fallback when an agent has an exact, unique identifier like an account number.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reason I'd reach for SOSL here instead of five SOQL queries is that this is fundamentally a search problem, not a lookup problem — the agent doesn't have an exact key, they've got a fuzzy human input like a partial name or phone number, and that's exactly what the search index is built for, versus five separate LIKE-based SOQL queries that would each be slow and would each eat into the same 100-query-per-transaction budget. But I wouldn't oversell SOSL as a free solution — it caps out at 2,000 total rows across everything you searched, so on a common name you might be looking at a capped, effectively random-looking subset, and I'd make sure the UI says 'top matches' instead of implying it found everything. The other thing that bites people is index latency — if an agent just created a record thirty seconds ago and immediately searches for it, there's a real chance it hasn't hit the search index yet, which is a confusing moment if nobody warned them about it. So in practice I'd use SOSL for the fast multi-object fuzzy search, keep the field list it searches tight and deliberate instead of 'every text field,' and still keep an exact-match SOQL lookup available for when an agent has something precise like an account number.
commonMistakes: Uses five parallel SOQL queries with LIKE '%value%' instead of a single SOSL call
Assumes SOSL returns a complete result set rather than being capped at 2,000 total rows
Doesn't account for search index latency on very recently created or updated records
Searches every text field on every object instead of a deliberately scoped field list
Doesn't provide an exact-match SOQL fallback for agents with a precise identifier
keyPoints: Correctly identifies SOSL's multi-object, index-based search as the architecturally correct fit
Explains why parallel SOQL with LIKE queries is worse at scale and against query limits
Names the 2,000-row cap and its real-world consequence for common search terms
Names search index latency as a real limitation for very recent records
Proposes scoping searchable fields deliberately and keeping an exact-match fallback

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why SOSL fits the multi-object fuzzy search use case
Names concrete SOSL limitations at enterprise scale (row cap, index latency)
Proposes a workable mitigation/design around those limitations

questions.title: CRM Analytics: Dataflow vs. Recipe vs. Data Sync
questions.prompt: Explain the architectural differences between a CRM Analytics Dataflow, a Recipe, and Data Sync, and when an enterprise analytics architecture should use each one rather than defaulting to whichever is easiest to build first.
questions.modelAnswer: Data Sync is the mechanism that replicates Salesforce object data (and, with connectors, some external data) into the CRM Analytics data store as-is, on a schedule, with minimal transformation — it's the foundation almost every dataset needs, but it's not an analytics transformation tool by itself, it's the ingestion layer. A Recipe is the modern, UI-driven, node-based transformation tool built on a more efficient Spark-based execution engine, supporting joins, bucketing, column transformations, and now most of what Dataflows historically did, with faster iteration and a clearer visual lineage, and is the default choice for new transformation logic going forward since Salesforce has been consolidating investment there. A Dataflow is the older, JSON-defined transformation pipeline that predates Recipes; it still exists and still runs in many orgs' legacy pipelines, supports some transformation patterns that took longer to reach Recipes (certain advanced augment/filter sequences), and is still relevant to know because enterprise orgs with years of existing CRM Analytics investment often have substantial Dataflow logic that hasn't been migrated yet — understanding both is necessary to maintain that legacy investment during a transition period, not because Dataflow is the architecturally preferred choice for new work. For an enterprise data architecture, I'd default new transformation work to Recipes for the performance and maintainability gains, maintain and gradually migrate existing Dataflow logic rather than leaving a split-brain pipeline indefinitely, and treat Data Sync configuration itself as an architecture decision, not a default — deciding deliberately which objects and fields actually need to land in the analytics platform (rather than syncing everything), because over-syncing bloats dataset size, slows recipe run time, and creates its own governance and PII-exposure surface that a narrower, deliberate sync avoids.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the three as ingestion versus two generations of transformation. Data Sync is just how data actually gets from Salesforce objects into the analytics data store — it's not doing any real transformation, it's the plumbing every pipeline needs. Recipes are the newer, Spark-based transformation tool, and that's what I'd default new work to, because it's faster to iterate in and Salesforce has clearly been putting its investment there. Dataflows are the older JSON-based pipeline — I wouldn't build new logic in one, but I also wouldn't pretend they don't matter, because plenty of enterprise orgs have years of Dataflow logic running in production that somebody still has to understand and maintain during the transition to Recipes. The part I'd actually push on as an architect, though, is the Data Sync configuration itself — teams default to syncing every field on every object because it's the path of least resistance, and that's a real mistake: it bloats the dataset, slows down every recipe that reads from it, and creates a bigger PII surface than the analytics use case actually needs. I'd rather deliberately scope what gets synced to what the recipes genuinely consume.
commonMistakes: Treats Dataflow as the current best-practice transformation tool for new work
Doesn't distinguish Data Sync (ingestion) from Recipe/Dataflow (transformation)
Syncs every field on every object by default instead of deliberately scoping the sync
Ignores legacy Dataflow investment that still needs maintenance during a transition
Has no plan for migrating existing Dataflow logic to Recipes over time
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes Data Sync as ingestion from Recipe/Dataflow as transformation
Correctly identifies Recipes as the current default for new transformation work
Acknowledges legacy Dataflow investment as a real, still-relevant maintenance concern
Treats Data Sync field/object scoping as a deliberate architecture decision, not a default
Proposes a gradual migration path rather than an abrupt rewrite or indefinite split-brain state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the architectural role of each of the three
Recommends Recipes for new work while respecting legacy Dataflow reality
Treats Data Sync scope as a deliberate architecture decision

questions.title: Big Objects: When They're the Right Answer and Their Real Limitations
questions.prompt: A client wants to retain 10 years of case interaction history for compliance, well beyond what they're willing to keep as standard, reportable Case-related records. Explain when a Big Object is actually the correct architecture here, and the real limitations around async SOQL and indexing that come with that choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Big Objects are the correct choice when the data needs to be retained at very high volume (they're built for hundreds of millions to billions of records) for record-keeping, audit, or compliance purposes, where the access pattern is occasional, targeted lookup rather than frequent interactive reporting, list views, or roll-up aggregation — which matches a 10-year compliance retention requirement almost exactly, because that data is rarely touched day-to-day but must be retrievable and provably retained. The real limitation that surprises people is that Big Objects only support asynchronous SOQL queries by default for most operations, meaning you can't just drop a Big Object into a standard report, list view, or most declarative tools the way you would a standard or custom object — querying it typically requires Apex (async SOQL via Database.getAsyncLocator or similar, or the newer synchronous support that exists for specific limited query shapes against indexed fields) and a defined index on the fields you'll filter against, which must be planned at object creation time since Big Object indexes can't be added or changed as freely as on standard objects. This means the UI/UX for retrieving that 10 years of history generally can't be a standard Salesforce list view or report — it needs a custom Lightning component or Apex-backed interface built specifically to query the Big Object by its indexed key fields, which is a real development cost the client needs to understand upfront, not a feature parity swap for a regular object. Architecturally, the right pattern is: keep recent, actively-used case interaction data on a standard, reportable object (or a skinny table/appropriately indexed custom object) for whatever window the business actually works with daily, archive older records into the Big Object on a scheduled batch process once they age out of that active window, and build a narrow, purpose-built retrieval UI for the rare compliance-lookup or audit-response scenario rather than trying to make the archive feel like a normal reportable object.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the client that a Big Object is the right call here specifically because this data isn't something anyone's going to look at every day — it's compliance retention, which is exactly the access pattern Big Objects are built for: huge volume, rare and targeted lookups, not interactive reporting. But I'd be upfront about the real cost before they commit: you can't just drop a Big Object into a normal list view or report the way you would a custom object. Most access needs to go through Apex using asynchronous SOQL, and the fields you'll ever need to filter on have to be indexed from the start, because you can't casually add indexes later the way you can on a regular object. So the realistic design is a two-tier setup — recent case interactions stay on a normal, reportable object where people actually work day to day, and once records age past that window, a scheduled batch job archives them into the Big Object. And when compliance or an auditor actually needs something from ten years back, that's a purpose-built lookup screen, not a report — I wouldn't let anyone assume this feels the same as querying a regular object, because it doesn't.
commonMistakes: Assumes a Big Object supports standard reports, list views, and roll-ups like a regular object
Doesn't plan indexed fields at object creation time, before volume makes that impossible to retrofit cheaply
Tries to use Big Objects for data that actually needs frequent interactive access
Underestimates the custom development cost of a purpose-built retrieval UI
Has no tiered archiving process moving aged records from the active object into the Big Object
keyPoints: Correctly identifies Big Objects as suited to high-volume, rarely-accessed compliance/audit data
Explains the async SOQL requirement and its UI/UX implications
Explains that indexes must be planned at creation time, not added freely later
Proposes a tiered design: active object plus scheduled archiving into the Big Object
Sets accurate expectations about custom development cost for retrieval

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies when a Big Object is the right architectural fit
Accurately explains async SOQL and indexing limitations
Proposes a workable tiered archiving design

questions.title: Deterministic vs. Probabilistic Encryption's Effect on Reporting
questions.prompt: A newly encrypted Account Number field (deterministic mode) is now showing inconsistent behavior: it filters correctly in a report but a related list view's sort by that column silently stopped working, and a formula field referencing it broke. Explain exactly what's happening and what can and can't be fixed.
questions.modelAnswer: Deterministic encryption does preserve equality comparisons, which is why exact-match report filters on that field continue to work, but it does not preserve ordering — the encrypted ciphertext's sort order bears no relationship to the plaintext value's natural sort order, so a list view sort on an encrypted field, even in deterministic mode, will sort by ciphertext, which looks broken because it doesn't match the human expectation of alphanumeric or numeric order; this isn't a bug, it's an inherent property of how the encryption preserves equality but not range/order. The formula field breaking is a separate, well-documented limitation: formula fields have a restricted, explicitly documented set of operators and functions that work against encrypted fields at all (certain text functions and most comparison operators beyond simple equality aren't supported), so a formula that worked against the plaintext field before encryption was turned on may use an operator that simply isn't supported against an encrypted source field and needs to be rewritten, or in some cases can't be replicated at all without decrypting the data in Apex instead of in a formula. The fix for the list-view sort is, honestly, that there generally isn't a clean fix within declarative list views if the field remains encrypted — sort-by-ciphertext is going to look wrong to users as long as the field is encrypted, so the real decision is whether the sort requirement is important enough to either move it to a different, non-encrypted helper field (if compliance allows storing a non-sensitive sortable proxy), or to accept the UX tradeoff as the cost of encrypting that field, and that's a decision for the compliance owner, not something an admin can engineer around with declarative tools alone. The formula should be audited function-by-function against Salesforce's documented list of encrypted-field-compatible operators, and anything unsupported needs to move into Apex (which can call a method to decrypt and evaluate server-side with appropriate field-level security) or be redesigned to avoid needing that computation on the encrypted value directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The report filter working but the sort breaking is actually consistent, even though it feels contradictory — deterministic encryption preserves whether two values are equal, which is exactly what an exact-match filter needs, but it does nothing to preserve order, so when you sort by that column you're sorting by ciphertext, which has no relationship to what the plaintext numbers would look like sorted. That's not something I can fix declaratively while the field stays encrypted — I'd tell the business that's the real tradeoff of encrypting this field, and the actual decision is whether that broken-looking sort is acceptable, or whether we need a separate, non-sensitive proxy field to sort by instead, and that's a call for whoever owns compliance, not something I'd quietly engineer around. The formula breaking is a different issue — formula fields only support a specific, documented set of operations against encrypted fields, so whatever that formula was doing probably used something outside that supported list. I'd go operator by operator against Salesforce's documented compatibility list, and anything that isn't supported has to move into Apex, where I can decrypt and evaluate it in code with the right field-level security checks, instead of trying to force it through a formula that was never built to handle that operation on ciphertext.
commonMistakes: Treats the broken sort order as a bug rather than an inherent property of encrypted ciphertext
Assumes deterministic encryption preserving equality also preserves ordering
Doesn't check Salesforce's documented list of formula operators compatible with encrypted fields
Tries to 'fix' the sort declaratively instead of recognizing it requires a business/compliance decision
Moves the broken formula logic into Apex without re-evaluating field-level security on the decrypted value
keyPoints: Correctly explains why deterministic encryption preserves equality but not sort order
Correctly diagnoses the formula break as an unsupported operator/function against an encrypted field
Recognizes the sort-order issue has no clean declarative fix while the field stays encrypted
Frames the sort-order tradeoff as a compliance-owned decision, not an admin workaround
Proposes moving unsupported formula logic into properly secured Apex

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why equality filtering still works but sort order doesn't
Correctly diagnoses the formula break as an unsupported operator issue
Correctly frames the sort-order issue as a business/compliance decision, not a bug to fix
Proposes a sound path for the formula logic (Apex with proper security)

questions.title: Data Skew at Enterprise Scale and Sharing Recalculation Cost
questions.prompt: Explain what ownership skew and account (parent) skew actually are, why they cause disproportionate sharing recalculation cost at enterprise scale, and what specific mitigations exist for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Ownership skew occurs when a very large number of records (commonly over 10,000) are owned by a single user, which causes problems specifically when that user's role changes, is deactivated, or their role hierarchy position moves, because every one of those records' sharing needs to be recalculated against the new position — the recalculation job isn't proportional to typical workload, it's proportional to how many records that one user owns, so a single ownership change can trigger a sharing recalculation touching millions of rows. Account (parent) skew occurs when a very large number of child records (commonly over 10,000) roll up to a single parent record, like one Account with hundreds of thousands of child Opportunities or Cases, which causes problems specifically around locking: when implicit sharing rules grant access to child records based on the parent's sharing, and especially when the parent record itself is being updated, Salesforce needs to lock and process sharing for all of those children, which both slows that specific transaction and increases lock contention risk if multiple processes try to touch records under that same skewed parent concurrently. The mitigation for ownership skew is to avoid assigning huge numbers of records to one owner in the first place (route them to a queue instead of an individual user where ownership itself doesn't need to carry the sharing logic the same way, since queue membership changes don't trigger the same recalculation cascade), and when an existing skewed owner's role must change, do it through Salesforce Support's recommended data skew mitigation process or during a planned low-traffic window with mass transfer tools designed for this rather than a direct role hierarchy edit. The mitigation for account skew is to avoid the default implicit sharing model that cascades from a skewed parent (consider restricting sharing to the parent level and not extending it implicitly to a child object with enormous skew, or using a separate junction/intermediate object to break the direct parent-child volume relationship), and at genuinely large scale this is also where deferred sharing calculation (temporarily disabling automatic sharing recalculation during a mass data load or reparenting operation, performing the operation, then recalculating once) becomes a necessary tool rather than letting every individual DML in a bulk load trigger its own recalculation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain both of these as the same underlying problem wearing different clothes — a tiny number of records or users ending up with a wildly disproportionate share of the relationships that drive sharing recalculation. Ownership skew is when one user owns way more records than anyone else, and the danger isn't day-to-day use, it's the moment that user's role changes or they get deactivated — now the system has to recalculate sharing on every single record they own, all at once, and that job scales with however many records that one person has, not with normal traffic. Account skew is the parent-side version — one Account with hundreds of thousands of child records, and now any operation that touches sharing on that parent, or implicit sharing that cascades to the children, has to deal with that whole pile at once, which is also exactly the kind of thing that causes lock contention if anything else tries to touch those same records at the same time. For ownership skew, my go-to fix is routing high-volume records to a queue instead of a person in the first place, and if an existing skewed owner's role does need to change, doing it through a planned, supported mass-transfer process, not a casual role edit. For account skew, I'd look hard at whether that implicit sharing cascade to the children is even necessary, and at real scale I'd use deferred sharing calculation during a bulk load or reparenting operation so I'm not recalculating sharing on every single row as it's loaded, only once at the end.
commonMistakes: Doesn't distinguish ownership skew (owner-side) from account/parent skew (child-volume-side)
Treats a role hierarchy change on a skewed owner as a routine operation with no special handling
Doesn't recognize implicit sharing cascade from a skewed parent as a lock contention risk
Doesn't know deferred sharing calculation exists as a mitigation for bulk loads/reparenting
Recommends assigning high-volume records to individual users instead of queues
keyPoints: Correctly defines ownership skew and its sharing-recalculation trigger (role/ownership changes)
Correctly defines account/parent skew and its locking/implicit-sharing cascade risk
Recommends queue-based ownership over individual-user ownership for high-volume records
Recommends a planned, supported process for role changes on existing skewed owners
Names deferred sharing calculation as a mitigation for bulk loads and reparenting operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains ownership skew and its specific recalculation trigger
Correctly explains account/parent skew and its locking risk
Proposes concrete, correct mitigations for ownership skew
Proposes concrete, correct mitigations for account skew

questions.title: Consolidating Six Triggers into a Bulkified Domain Handler Framework
questions.prompt: An Account object has six separate triggers written by different contractors over the years, with no defined order and overlapping responsibilities. Sketch the handler-framework skeleton you'd refactor them into, and explain how it guarantees bulk safety and a predictable execution order.
questions.modelAnswer: The refactor collapses six triggers into exactly one trigger per object that does nothing but delegate to a single handler class extending a shared base (TriggerHandlerBase) that exposes one override method per context (beforeInsert, beforeUpdate, afterUpdate, and so on), so there is now exactly one place that owns execution order within each context instead of six triggers whose relative order Salesforce doesn't guarantee and nobody controls. Each override method calls into domain-layer static methods (AccountDomain) that each take the full trigger list and old map as bulk collections, never a single record, which forces every piece of logic that used to assume 'one record at a time' in the original six triggers to be rewritten as a loop-once, no-nested-query pattern. Bulk safety comes from a hard rule baked into the base class and code review: no SOQL or DML inside a loop anywhere in the domain methods, every related-record lookup is done once via a map built from a single bulk query keyed by the trigger records' IDs, and any method that needs to call another domain's logic (publishing events, cross-object updates) does so by appending to a shared, trigger-context-scoped collection that gets processed once at the end of the handler rather than firing immediately inline, which also helps control recursion. The predictable order comes from the handler method body itself being an explicit, read-top-to-bottom sequence of domain method calls, so 'what runs first' is answered by reading five lines of code in one file, not by guessing at six triggers' undocumented relative firing order, and any new automation on this object from now on has to be added as a call inside this one handler rather than as trigger number seven.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd fix isn't bulkification, it's that there's no single place anyone can read to answer 'what order does this stuff run in' — with six triggers, Salesforce doesn't guarantee or document their relative order, so that's effectively undefined behavior that happens to work today. So step one is collapsing to exactly one trigger per object, calling one handler class, with one override method per context, so the order is just whatever order I wrote the method calls in, in one file I can read top to bottom. Then for bulk safety, I move everything into domain-layer static methods that take the whole list and old map, never a single record, and I enforce — in code review, not just as a guideline — that nothing in there runs a SOQL query or a DML statement inside a loop; any related data gets pulled once as a map keyed by ID and then read from memory. And because contractors over the years is exactly how you end up with hidden recursion, I'd also make sure any downstream event or cross-object update gets collected into a list and processed once at the end of the handler, rather than fired inline wherever it happens to be written, so it's much harder for one update to accidentally retrigger another automation that retriggers this one again.
commonMistakes: Keeps multiple triggers per object instead of consolidating to exactly one trigger calling one handler
Writes domain methods that still process one record at a time instead of bulk collections
Runs SOQL or DML inside a loop within the consolidated domain logic
Fires cross-object updates or events inline instead of collecting and processing once per transaction
Has no explicit, readable statement of execution order within each trigger context
keyPoints: Consolidates to exactly one trigger per object delegating to one handler class
Enforces bulk-safe domain methods operating on full lists/maps, never single records
Bans SOQL/DML inside loops as a hard rule, not a guideline
Makes execution order explicit and readable in one place
Batches cross-object side effects to reduce recursion risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct, bulk-safe handler/domain skeleton
Explains how execution order becomes explicit and predictable
Explains concrete bulk-safety enforcement (no SOQL/DML in loops)
Addresses recursion risk from cross-object side effects

questions.title: Queueable Chaining with a Finalizer for Guaranteed Cleanup
questions.prompt: Write the skeleton of a Queueable job that chains itself across multiple batches of work and uses a Finalizer to guarantee a failure gets logged even if the job dies with an unhandled exception, rather than failing silently.
questions.modelAnswer: A Finalizer attached via System.attachFinalizer(this) inside execute() is guaranteed to run after the Queueable finishes, whether it succeeded or threw an unhandled exception, which is exactly the gap plain Queueable chaining has on its own — without it, an exception in batch 47 of 200 just stops the chain silently, and nothing downstream ever finds out batch 48 through 200 never ran. The Finalizer's execute(FinalizerContext) method checks ctx.getResult() against ParentJobResult.UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION specifically, and on that branch writes a durable record (a custom object row, not just a debug log) capturing which batch index failed and the exception detail, which is the piece that turns 'job silently stopped' into 'here's exactly what failed and where to resume.' This pattern also respects the governor limit on chain depth implicitly: because each job only enqueues the next one from inside its own execute(), the 50-queued-jobs-per-transaction ceiling isn't the relevant limit here (that applies to jobs enqueued synchronously within a single executing context, not sequential chaining), but the daily async Apex execution ceiling for the whole org still applies, so the backlog table doubles as the mechanism for resuming tomorrow if today's run gets cut off by that org-wide ceiling. I'd also make the Finalizer idempotent-safe on its own write (checking whether a backlog row for this batchIndex already exists) since a Finalizer re-attached during a retry scenario shouldn't create duplicate backlog rows.
questions.professionalAnswer: The piece I wouldn't skip here is the Finalizer, because plain Queueable chaining has a real blind spot — if batch 47 out of 200 throws an unhandled exception, the chain just stops, and unless someone happens to notice reconciliation data looks wrong three days later, nobody knows it died early. Attaching a Finalizer inside execute() guarantees something runs afterward no matter what, success or failure, so in its FinalizerContext callback I check whether the result was an unhandled exception specifically, and if so I write that failure, with the batch index and exception detail, into an actual backlog table — not just a debug log that nobody's watching. That backlog table is also doing double duty: if the whole run gets cut off because the org hit its daily async execution ceiling, that's where tomorrow's run picks up from instead of starting over or silently skipping whatever didn't finish. And I'd make sure the backlog write itself checks for an existing row for that batch index first, because if this ever gets retried, I don't want duplicate failure records piling up.
commonMistakes: Chains Queueable jobs without attaching a Finalizer, leaving failures silent
Logs failures only to debug logs instead of a durable, queryable backlog record
Confuses the 50-enqueue-per-transaction limit with the org-wide daily async execution ceiling
Doesn't make the Finalizer's backlog write idempotent against retries
Has no resumption strategy for a chain cut off by hitting a daily governor limit
keyPoints: Attaches a Finalizer via System.attachFinalizer to guarantee post-execution handling
Correctly checks ParentJobResult.UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION in the Finalizer callback
Writes failures to a durable, queryable backlog object, not just debug logs
Correctly distinguishes the per-transaction enqueue limit from the daily async ceiling
Designs the backlog as a resumption mechanism, not just a log

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the Queueable/Finalizer pattern
Explains why the Finalizer closes a real silent-failure gap
Correctly reasons about relevant governor limits
Designs the backlog for durable resumption, not just logging

questions.title: Bulk-Publishing High-Volume Platform Events Correctly
questions.prompt: A batch job processes 50,000 delayed shipment records and needs to notify downstream systems via a custom Platform Event. Write the correct bulk publishing pattern and explain what specifically goes wrong if you publish inside the per-record loop instead.
questions.modelAnswer: EventBus.publish accepts a List of event sObjects and should be called once per reasonably-sized batch (chunked to the platform's per-call maximum, typically processed in batches of up to a few thousand to stay well under per-transaction limits), building the full list of event records in memory first and publishing them together, which lets the platform handle delivery as one bulk operation instead of 50,000 separate publish calls. Calling EventBus.publish(singleEvent) inside the per-record loop instead does several things wrong at once: it burns one unit of whatever the relevant daily published-event allocation is per call rather than amortizing overhead across a bulk call, it makes error handling per-record instead of batch-level (so a single bad record's publish failure has to be caught and handled 50,000 times instead of once against a returned SaveResult list), and inside a Batch Apex execute() method operating on a scope of 200 records at a time, doing 200 individual publish calls per batch execution is far more likely to approach CPU time and heap limits than one bulk call with 200 events. The SaveResult list returned by the bulk publish call needs to be checked per element, because a bulk publish can partially succeed — some events in the list can fail validation or exceed a per-transaction limit while others succeed, and silently ignoring that returned list means some delayed-shipment notifications simply never reach downstream systems with no visible failure anywhere. I'd also log failed publishes to a durable object rather than just a debug statement, exactly like the Queueable backlog pattern, since 'delivery notification silently failed' for even a small percentage of 50,000 records is a real operational gap if nobody's watching for it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd absolutely not do is call EventBus.publish once per record inside that loop — I've seen that mistake specifically because single-event publish code looks fine in a small test with ten records and then falls over at real volume. The right pattern is to build the whole list of event sObjects in memory first, across the batch, and make one EventBus.publish call with the full list, which is both much more efficient and gives me back one SaveResult list I can check instead of needing to wrap every single publish call in its own error handling. And I wouldn't skip checking that returned SaveResult list item by item, because a bulk publish can partially succeed — some events can fail while most go through — and if I don't check it, some fraction of these delayed-shipment notifications just quietly never make it to whatever downstream system is supposed to react to them, and nobody finds out until someone asks why they never got notified.
commonMistakes: Calls EventBus.publish once per record inside the loop instead of once per batch
Ignores the returned SaveResult list, missing partial-failure cases
Logs publish failures only to debug statements instead of a durable, queryable record
Doesn't account for per-transaction publish allocation limits when sizing the batch
Assumes a successful call to EventBus.publish means every event in the list was delivered
keyPoints: Builds the full event list in memory and calls EventBus.publish once per batch
Checks the returned SaveResult list for partial failures, not just the overall call
Logs failed publishes to a durable, queryable object
Understands bulk publish can partially succeed
Correctly explains the cost of per-record publish calls at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the bulk EventBus.publish pattern
Explains concretely what breaks with per-record publishing
Correctly handles partial-failure SaveResult checking

questions.title: Batch Apex with a Custom QueryLocator for LDV Archiving
questions.prompt: Write a Batch Apex class that archives Cases closed more than two years ago into a Big Object, using a custom QueryLocator safe against large data volumes, and explain the governor-limit reasoning behind your scope size choice.
questions.modelAnswer: A custom QueryLocator backing the start() method lets Batch Apex iterate the full result set in chunks without ever holding more than one batch's worth of records in heap at a time, and critically it supports up to 50 million records, versus the much lower row limits of an Iterable-based start() method, which matters directly for a Case object that could have millions of closed rows going back years. The scope size (passed as the optional second argument to Database.executeBatch, defaulting to 200) is a tradeoff between throughput and per-batch governor limits: each execute() invocation gets its own fresh set of governor limits, so a larger scope (say 2,000) processes more records per invocation and reduces total overhead, but it also means more records' worth of DML, CPU, and heap need to fit inside that one execute() call's limits — for a Big Object insert via Database.insertImmediate, which is itself a synchronous, non-DML-limit-counted style write path, a larger batch size is often safe, but if execute() also did additional per-record SOQL or callouts, I'd keep the scope smaller to stay safely under the per-batch limits. I used Database.insertImmediate for the Big Object write specifically because Big Object writes don't count against the standard 150 DML statements per transaction the same way, but the call is still synchronous and still has its own throughput characteristics worth testing at realistic volume before committing to a scope size. I also implemented Database.Stateful specifically because I need archivedCount to persist and accumulate across batch execute() invocations for the finish() method's completion notification — without Stateful, instance member variables reset to their initial value at the start of every single execute() call, which is a common mistake that silently produces a wrong final count.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two things I'd get right here before anything else: a real QueryLocator, not an Iterable, because an Iterable-based start method caps out far below what a multi-year Case backlog actually has, and Database.Stateful, because without it that archivedCount variable resets to zero at the start of every single batch execute call — I've seen that exact mistake produce a confidently wrong completion count nobody catches until someone cross-checks it. For scope size, I wouldn't just leave it at the default 200 without thinking about it, but I also wouldn't blindly maximize it — since this execute method is really just building records and doing one Big Object insert per batch, a bigger scope like 2,000 is probably safe and more efficient, but if this logic ever grows to include a callout or extra per-record queries, I'd want to dial that scope size back down so a single execute invocation doesn't come close to its own fresh governor limits. And for the actual archive write, I'd use Database.insertImmediate against the Big Object specifically because that write path doesn't eat into the standard 150-DML-statement ceiling the way a normal insert would.
commonMistakes: Uses an Iterable-based start() method instead of a true QueryLocator, capping out at far fewer records
Omits Database.Stateful while relying on an instance variable to accumulate across batches
Picks a batch scope size without reasoning about what else execute() does per record
Uses a standard DML insert for the Big Object write instead of Database.insertImmediate
Doesn't test the chosen scope size against realistic data volume before committing to it in production
keyPoints: Implements a real Database.QueryLocator, not an Iterable, for LDV safety
Correctly implements Database.Stateful to accumulate a running count across batches
Reasons about scope size as a tradeoff tied to what execute() actually does per record
Uses Database.insertImmediate correctly for the Big Object write
Understands execute() gets fresh governor limits per invocation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements a QueryLocator-based, Stateful batch class
Correctly implements the Big Object archive write
Gives sound governor-limit reasoning for the scope size choice

questions.title: An LWC Wire Adapter with Imperative Fallback and Caching for a High-Traffic Component
questions.prompt: A record-page component shows an account health summary computed server-side, rendered on every Account record page view across thousands of daily users. Write the LWC/Apex pattern you'd use to keep this fast and cache-friendly, and explain the caching behavior you're relying on.
questions.modelAnswer: The @wire adapter calling an @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) Apex method is the right choice for a read-only, record-page-scoped value like this because cacheable=true lets the Lightning Data Service client-side cache store the result keyed by the method and its parameters, so navigating back to an Account record page the user already viewed in this session can return the cached value without a new server round-trip, and multiple components on the same page requesting the same data share one cached result instead of each firing its own Apex call. The @api recordId combined with the reactive '$recordId' parameter binding means the wire automatically re-invokes the Apex method whenever the component is placed on a different record, without needing any imperative refresh logic, which is exactly the behavior wanted for a component reused across every Account page. A cacheable Apex method must not perform any DML and must be read-only in effect, which fits this use case naturally since computing a health summary is a pure read; if the requirement ever needed a guaranteed-fresh value immediately after an update on the same page, I'd pair this with an imperative call plus refreshApex() rather than relying on the wire's cache, but for a dashboard-style summary viewed by thousands of users daily, the caching behavior is the actual performance win, not a side effect to work around. At enterprise scale, the heavier optimization is making sure AccountHealthService.computeSummary itself is cheap and bulk-safe internally (no per-call SOQL inside loops, reasonable use of Apex's own platform cache if the computation is expensive and doesn't need to be instantly fresh), since the wire's client-side caching only helps repeat views by the same user in the same session, not the first load or a different user's first load of the same record.
questions.professionalAnswer: For something rendered on every single Account page view across thousands of users a day, I want the wire service calling a cacheable Apex method, not an imperative call fired from connectedCallback, specifically because cacheable=true lets Lightning Data Service cache the result client-side, so if this same user revisits an Account they already looked at, or another component on the page needs the exact same data, it doesn't need to go back to the server every time. Binding recordId reactively with the dollar-sign syntax means I don't have to write any manual refresh logic when the component gets reused on a different record — the wire handles that automatically. The thing I'd be careful about is that a cacheable method has to actually be read-only, no DML, which is naturally true here since I'm just computing a summary, but if I ever needed this to reflect a change the user just made on the same page, I wouldn't lean on the wire's caching for that — I'd use an imperative call with refreshApex instead, because the wire's cache is for repeat views, not guaranteed freshness immediately after a write. And honestly, at real scale, the component-level caching is only half the win — I'd also want to make sure the actual computation on the server side is cheap and bulk-safe, because the first time any given user loads any given record, that cache isn't helping them yet.
commonMistakes: Uses an imperative Apex call for a simple, reusable read instead of a cacheable wire adapter
Marks a method cacheable=true while it still performs DML, which isn't a valid use of the annotation
Writes manual refresh logic for recordId changes instead of using reactive '$recordId' binding
Relies on wire caching to guarantee fresh data immediately after an update on the same page
Ignores server-side computation cost, assuming client-side caching alone solves performance at scale
keyPoints: Uses @wire with a cacheable=true Apex method for the read-only summary
Uses reactive '$recordId' parameter binding instead of manual refresh logic
Correctly explains what cacheable=true requires (read-only, no DML) and what it buys
Knows when to use imperative call plus refreshApex instead of relying on wire caching
Also addresses server-side computation cost, not just client-side caching

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the wire/cacheable Apex pattern
Correctly explains the caching behavior and its limits
Knows when an imperative call plus refreshApex is the right alternative
Addresses server-side cost, not just client-side caching

questions.title: Resolving a Source-Tracking Conflict in a Scratch-Org-Based DX Pipeline
questions.prompt: Two developers working in separate scratch orgs both modified the same Page Layout and a shared Apex class, and their source-tracked pushes now conflict when merging into the integration branch. Walk through the actual procedure you'd follow to resolve this safely, not just 'pick one.'
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is never to blindly accept either developer's full file as the resolution; it's to pull both scratch orgs' retrieved source into git, diff them properly (sf project retrieve start against each org, or reviewing their already-pushed branches) and look at the actual metadata XML for the page layout and the actual Apex diff, because page layout XML in particular is highly order- and position-sensitive and a naive text merge can silently produce a layout that looks fine in the diff but renders incorrectly or drops a field the other developer added. For the Apex class conflict, since Apex is readable code, a standard three-way git merge usually resolves cleanly if the two developers touched different methods, but if they touched the same method, that needs an actual conversation about whose change reflects the current intended behavior, not an automatic merge tool decision, because git doesn't know which change is semantically correct, only that both touched the same lines. Once resolved, the merged result needs to be validated by creating a fresh scratch org from the current integration branch, deploying the merged source into it, and running the full relevant test class suite plus a manual check of the page layout in the UI, specifically because XML merge conflicts in metadata are notorious for merging syntactically validly while being semantically wrong (a field reference that resolves but points to the wrong section, for instance). Finally, I'd use this as the trigger for a process fix, not just a one-off resolution: flag that this page layout and this Apex class are evidently being modified by multiple developers concurrently without coordination, and either establish a convention (one owner per page layout, feature-flagged branches for Apex classes under active multi-developer work) or increase the frequency of integration-branch merges so conflicts surface in hours, not after two developers have diverged for days.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is not to just pick whichever push happened second, because with a page layout that's a great way to silently lose a field the other developer added without anyone noticing until someone complains weeks later. I'd actually pull both versions, look at the real metadata XML diff for the layout and the real code diff for the Apex class, and for the Apex side, if they touched different methods, a normal three-way git merge is usually fine — but if they touched the same method, that's not a merge tool decision, that's a five-minute conversation between the two developers about whose change is actually the current intended behavior. Either way, before I call it resolved, I spin up a fresh scratch org from the merged integration branch, deploy it, run the relevant tests, and actually open the page layout in the UI, because metadata XML can merge in a way that's syntactically valid but semantically wrong, and a green deploy doesn't prove the layout looks right. And since this is the second time I'm manually untangling a conflict on this same layout or class, I'd treat that as a signal — either this needs a clearer single owner, or we need to be merging to the integration branch more often so two people don't drift apart for days before anyone notices they're both touching the same thing.
commonMistakes: Resolves the conflict by blindly accepting one developer's full file without reviewing both
Treats a page layout XML merge conflict the same as a simple text merge with no semantic review
Lets an automatic merge tool resolve a same-method Apex conflict without a human conversation
Skips validating the merged result in a fresh scratch org before considering it resolved
Doesn't address the underlying process gap that let two developers diverge on the same files
keyPoints: Reviews both developers' actual metadata/code diffs rather than picking one side
Treats page layout XML conflicts as requiring semantic review, not just text merging
Escalates same-method Apex conflicts to a human conversation rather than an automatic merge
Validates the merged result in a fresh scratch org with tests and a manual UI check
Identifies and addresses the process gap that allowed the conflict to occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a safe, non-naive conflict resolution procedure
Correctly treats page layout XML conflicts as requiring semantic review
Validates the resolution in a fresh scratch org before trusting it
Addresses the underlying process gap, not just this one incident

questions.title: Implementing a Circuit Breaker for an Unreliable Outbound Callout
questions.prompt: An outbound REST callout to a partner's credit-check API has started failing intermittently, and every failure still costs the full callout timeout, which is now slowing down the Lightning action that depends on it. Write a circuit breaker pattern that fails fast once the dependency is clearly down, and explain how you'd reset it.
questions.modelAnswer: The core idea is tracking consecutive failure count and a circuit-open flag in a durable custom object (not a static variable, since static state doesn't persist across separate Apex transactions, which is what most callouts from a Lightning action actually are), so that once failures cross a threshold, the circuit flips open and every subsequent call for the cooldown period fails immediately with no actual HTTP call attempted, which is the entire point: a user clicking a Lightning action gets an immediate, predictable failure (and can be shown a friendly fallback UI) instead of waiting out a full callout timeout on a dependency that's already known to be down. The reset mechanism here is a simple time-based half-open check: once the cooldown window has elapsed, isCircuitOpen() flips the state back to closed optimistically and lets the next call through as a real test of whether the dependency has recovered — if that call succeeds, recordSuccess resets the failure counter; if it fails again, recordFailure immediately reopens the circuit and restarts the cooldown clock. This needs to be implemented carefully around Apex's lack of true shared mutable state across transactions: every state read and write goes through the custom object, which means the breaker's accuracy under concurrent Lightning actions depends on reasonably fast, small DML updates to that state record, and at very high concurrency you'd want to think about row-lock contention on that single state record as its own secondary scaling concern. I'd also make sure callers have an actual fallback behavior defined for the circuit-open case — showing a 'credit check temporarily unavailable, try again shortly' message rather than a raw exception — since the whole point of failing fast is to let the UI degrade gracefully, not just to throw a different exception faster.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem I'm solving is that every failed callout still costs the user the full timeout, so even though the API is clearly struggling, each user action waits out that whole timeout before failing — that's the opposite of a good user experience when the dependency is known to be unhealthy. So I track consecutive failures and an open/closed flag on an actual custom object, not a static variable, because static variables don't survive between the separate transactions these Lightning action callouts actually run in. Once failures cross a threshold, the circuit opens, and every call for a cooldown window fails immediately with no real HTTP call attempted at all — that's the entire value of the pattern, trading a slow failure for an instant one. To reset it, I don't need anything fancy — once the cooldown window passes, I let exactly one call through as a real test; if it succeeds, the failure counter resets and the circuit stays closed, and if it fails, it reopens immediately and the cooldown clock restarts. The thing I'd make sure the calling code actually does with an open-circuit exception is show a real fallback message to the user, not just a different flavor of error, because the whole reason I built this was to make failure fast and graceful, not just fast.
commonMistakes: Tracks circuit state in a static Apex variable instead of a durable, cross-transaction custom object
Has no cooldown/half-open mechanism, leaving the circuit permanently open once tripped
Lets every call still attempt the full HTTP request even while the circuit is open
Doesn't provide a graceful fallback UI/behavior for the circuit-open case
Ignores row-lock contention risk on the shared state record under high concurrency
keyPoints: Tracks failure count and open state in a durable custom object, not static Apex state
Implements a cooldown-based half-open retry to test recovery
Fails fast with no real HTTP call attempted while the circuit is open
Resets the failure counter on a successful probe call, reopens on failure
Pairs the pattern with a graceful fallback behavior for callers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements a durable circuit breaker pattern
Correctly explains the cooldown/reset (half-open) mechanism
Addresses concurrency/fallback considerations

questions.title: Writing a Selective SOQL Query Against a 5-Million-Row Custom Object
questions.prompt: A custom Transaction__c object has 5 million rows. Write a SOQL query that reliably stays selective when filtering by status and a date range, and explain exactly why the naive version of this query would not be selective at that volume.
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Transaction_Date__c, Amount__c, Status__c
FROM Transaction__c
WHERE Status__c = 'Pending'
AND Transaction_Date__c >= :startDate
AND Transaction_Date__c < :endDate
ORDER BY Transaction_Date__c DESC
LIMIT 2000
questions.modelAnswer: The naive version of this query, filtering on Status__c alone, is likely not selective at 5 million rows because Status__c is a low-cardinality picklist-style field — if Pending represents even 15-20% of all rows, that's well above the roughly 10% (of the first million rows, tightening further above that) selectivity threshold the query optimizer uses to decide whether to use an index or fall back to a full table scan, so a single-condition filter on status alone would likely force a table scan across all 5 million rows even with a custom index requested on that field. Combining Status__c with a genuinely narrow Transaction_Date__c range makes the compound filter selective even though Status__c alone wasn't, because the date range condition, if the window is reasonably tight (a day, a week, a specific fiscal period) and Transaction_Date__c is indexed, can itself narrow the candidate set well below the threshold, and the query optimizer evaluates compound filter selectivity jointly, not just on the single most selective condition in isolation. Requesting a custom index on Transaction_Date__c (a standard custom field doesn't get one automatically the way CreatedDate does) from Salesforce Support, or using a custom index on a compound field if the filter pattern is consistent, is a necessary prerequisite here — selectivity math only matters if there's an index for the optimizer to actually choose to use. Finally, I added an explicit LIMIT to this query because at 5 million rows and growing, a query with no LIMIT that happens to become non-selective again as data grows (say, if Pending transactions become a larger share of the table over time) degrades silently rather than failing loudly, and a bounded result set with pagination, if the UI needs more than 2,000 rows, is safer than trusting selectivity to hold indefinitely as the table grows.
questions.professionalAnswer: The naive version of this — just filtering by Status__c equals Pending — is almost certainly not selective at 5 million rows, because a status field is low cardinality, and if Pending is even a modest chunk of the table, that's well above the roughly 10% selectivity threshold the optimizer uses to decide between an index scan and a full table scan. What makes it selective is pairing that with a genuinely narrow date range — the optimizer looks at the combined filter, not just the worst one in isolation, so if the date window is tight and Transaction_Date__c is actually indexed, that compound filter together comes in well under the threshold even though Status__c alone never would. And I'd flag that Transaction_Date__c being a custom field means it doesn't get an index automatically the way CreatedDate does — that's something I'd need to request from Salesforce Support if it isn't already there, because selectivity math is pointless if there's no index behind the field in the first place. I also put a LIMIT on this deliberately, because at 5 million rows and climbing, I don't want to assume this stays selective forever as the data grows — I'd rather bound the result set and paginate if the UI genuinely needs more than that.
commonMistakes: Filters only on the low-cardinality Status__c field, assuming that alone is selective
Doesn't request or verify a custom index exists on Transaction_Date__c
Writes an unbounded query with no LIMIT, trusting selectivity to hold indefinitely as data grows
Assumes the optimizer evaluates only the single most selective filter instead of the compound filter
Doesn't recognize that a query selective today can become non-selective as data distribution shifts
keyPoints: Correctly identifies why Status__c alone is not selective at this volume
Correctly explains why pairing it with a narrow date range achieves joint selectivity
Knows custom fields require a requested custom index, unlike CreatedDate
Adds a LIMIT as a defensive measure against future selectivity degradation
Reasons about selectivity as a property of the data distribution, not just the query syntax

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly structured, selective SOQL query
Correctly explains why the naive single-filter version fails
Correctly explains indexing prerequisites and the LIMIT safeguard

questions.title: Constructing a Multi-Object SOSL Query for a Global Search Feature
questions.prompt: Write a SOSL query that lets a service agent search for a phone number fragment across Contact, Lead, and Account simultaneously, returning only the fields the UI actually needs, and explain the tradeoff of how many fields you return.
questions.code:
FIND {555-0142*} IN PHONE FIELDS
RETURNING
    Contact(Id, Name, Phone, AccountId, Email),
    Lead(Id, Name, Phone, Company, Status),
    Account(Id, Name, Phone, BillingCity)
LIMIT 50
questions.modelAnswer: The FIND clause uses a wildcard-suffixed phrase against PHONE FIELDS specifically, which scopes the search to phone-type fields across the three objects rather than searching every text field on every object, which both improves relevance (no noisy matches from unrelated text fields) and keeps the search index lookup cheap relative to an ALL FIELDS search. The RETURNING clause lists each object with only the specific fields the UI actually renders, which matters for two reasons: first, SOSL's overall row return behavior and per-transaction heap cost both benefit from a narrower field list, since every additional field returned across every matched row adds up at the row counts this kind of global search can realistically return; second, returning extra fields 'just in case' is a common habit that silently grows over time as different developers add one more field to the same query, and at a shared, high-traffic global search endpoint that habit compounds into real performance cost. The explicit LIMIT 50 here is deliberate and separate from the platform's overall 2,000-row SOSL cap across all returned objects combined — a tighter UI-appropriate limit avoids ever hitting that platform ceiling in a way that would otherwise require the UI to handle an ambiguous 'results were capped' state, and 50 results is a reasonable number for a human agent to actually scan, versus a global 2,000-row cap that's really there to bound worst-case cost, not to suggest 2,000 results is a usable UI result set. If the search needs to expand to more objects or fields later, I'd push back on just appending to one query and instead reconsider whether a single SOSL call is still the right shape, since searching more and more objects in one call increases the chance any one of them dominates the shared 50-row-or-2,000-row budget and crowds out matches from the others.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd scope the FIND clause to PHONE FIELDS specifically rather than ALL FIELDS, because this is a phone number search, and searching every text field on three objects for a phone-number-shaped string is both slower and noisier — I'd rather get clean, relevant matches than cast the widest possible net. For the RETURNING clause, I'd be deliberate about only pulling the fields the UI actually renders, because I've seen 'just in case' fields pile up over time on a shared search query until it's returning twice what it needs to, and at a high-traffic endpoint like global search, that adds up. I also put an explicit LIMIT of 50 on it, separate from the platform's overall 2,000-row cap across everything SOSL returns — 50 is a number an agent can actually scan, and I'd rather hit my own deliberate limit than let the UI have to explain an ambiguous 'results got capped somewhere around 2,000' situation. And if this search ever needs to grow to more objects, I wouldn't just bolt them onto the same query without rethinking it, because every object I add is competing for the same shared result budget, and I don't want a common match on object four crowding out the three objects that actually matter most for this use case.

Returns every available field on each object instead of only what the UI renders
Relies on the platform's 2,000-row cap instead of a deliberate, UI-appropriate LIMIT
Doesn't recognize that returned-field bloat compounds over time on shared queries
Adds more objects to the same SOSL query without considering shared result-budget crowding
keyPoints: Scopes FIND to the relevant field category (PHONE FIELDS) rather than ALL FIELDS
Returns only the fields the UI actually needs per object
Applies a deliberate, UI-appropriate LIMIT distinct from the platform's overall row cap
Understands field-list bloat as a real, compounding performance cost over time
Reasons about result-budget crowding when considering adding more objects to the query
