questions.title: Loading Two Million Records with Bulk API 2.0 and Real Error Handling
questions.prompt: Describe and sketch the Bulk API 2.0 job pattern you'd use to load 2 million records into Salesforce from an external system, including how you'd detect and handle partial record-level failures within a job rather than just checking whether the overall job succeeded.
questions.modelAnswer: Bulk API 2.0 handles the chunking of a large CSV into internal batches automatically once the job is created and the file is uploaded and the job is marked UploadComplete, which removes the need to manually split 2 million records into 10,000-row batches the way Bulk API 1.0 required, but it does not remove the need to check per-record outcomes — a job can report an overall status of JobComplete while still containing a meaningful percentage of individual record failures, because 'the job ran' and 'every record succeeded' are two different things entirely. The correct pattern pulls both the successfulResults and failedResults endpoints explicitly after the job completes, because the failedResults CSV contains the specific error message and the original row data for every record that failed, which is what actually lets you build a remediation file rather than just knowing 'some records failed' with no actionable detail. At 2 million records, I'd also design for restart-ability from the start: track which source-system batch or file chunk each uploaded CSV corresponds to in an external tracking table (or the equivalent metadata on the migration side), so that if the job itself fails outright, or if a meaningful percentage of failedResults turn out to be a data-quality issue that needs a source-side fix and a retry, the remediation is 'reload this specific known-bad subset,' not 're-run the entire 2 million record load and hope duplicates don't happen.' I'd also pick an External ID field for the object being loaded and use the upsert operation rather than insert wherever the source data has a stable natural key, specifically so a retry after a partial failure is naturally idempotent instead of risking duplicate records from reprocessing rows that actually succeeded the first time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct if someone just checked 'did the job say complete' is that Bulk API 2.0 absolutely can report an overall success while a real chunk of individual records inside it failed — those are two separate things, and I wouldn't trust a job status alone for 2 million records. So after the job finishes, I always pull both result sets explicitly, successfulResults and failedResults, because the failed one gives me the actual error message and the original row for every record that didn't make it, which is what I need to actually fix something instead of just knowing something broke. At this volume, I'd also build this to be restartable from day one — I'd track which source batch each uploaded chunk corresponds to, so if I need to retry a subset because of a data issue, I know exactly which rows to resend instead of re-running the whole 2 million and hoping I don't create duplicates. And wherever the source system has a stable natural key, I'd use upsert against an External ID field instead of plain insert, specifically so that if I do have to retry a partially-failed batch, reprocessing the records that actually succeeded the first time doesn't create a second copy of them.
commonMistakes: Checks only the overall job status instead of pulling successfulResults and failedResults explicitly
Has no plan for restarting or retrying a subset of records after a partial failure
Uses insert instead of upsert against an External ID, risking duplicates on retry
Manually chunks the CSV into small batches, duplicating work Bulk API 2.0 already handles
Treats 'JobComplete' status as equivalent to 'every record succeeded'
keyPoints: Correctly describes the Bulk API 2.0 job lifecycle (create, upload, UploadComplete, poll)
Explicitly pulls both successfulResults and failedResults rather than trusting overall job status
Designs for restart-ability by tracking source batches for targeted retries
Uses upsert against a stable External ID to make retries idempotent
Correctly distinguishes overall job completion from per-record success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Bulk API 2.0 job pattern
Correctly handles partial record-level failure detection
Designs for restart-ability and idempotent retries at scale

questions.title: Blending Salesforce and Snowflake Data in a CRM Analytics Recipe
questions.prompt: Walk through the actual build steps for a CRM Analytics Recipe that blends Salesforce Opportunity data with a Snowflake-sourced customer profitability table, producing a dataset an executive dashboard can consume, and call out where this is likely to break at enterprise scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The build starts with two separate Data Sync or connector-based ingestion steps: a standard Salesforce object sync for Opportunity (and whatever related objects, like Account, the blend needs for join keys), and a Snowflake connection configured through CRM Analytics' external data connector, which brings the profitability table into the analytics data store on its own sync schedule, independent from the Salesforce sync cadence. Inside the Recipe, the join step needs a reliable common key between the two sources — typically an Account-level or Customer-level identifier that exists in both systems, which means the Snowflake table needs to carry the Salesforce Account Id (or a mapped external ID) as a column, something that has to be arranged on the Snowflake/ETL side before the Recipe can join cleanly, not something the Recipe itself can invent. After the join, the Recipe applies whatever transformation logic the dashboard needs (bucketing profitability into tiers, aggregating at the Account level if the source grain is finer, renaming/casting fields for consistent display), and the output is registered as a dataset the executive dashboard's lens/dashboard components query directly. The places this breaks at enterprise scale: first, sync timing misalignment — if the Snowflake sync and the Salesforce sync run on different schedules, the join can silently combine Opportunity data from today with profitability data that's a day or more stale, which needs to be called out to the business as a known data-currency characteristic, not hidden; second, join key drift — if an Account gets merged, renamed, or re-keyed in Salesforce without the corresponding update flowing back to the Snowflake-side identifier, the join silently drops or mismatches rows with no error surfaced to anyone; third, as both source tables grow, a naive join without appropriate indexing or without first aggregating the Snowflake side to the right grain can slow Recipe run time significantly, so I'd aggregate the high-volume Snowflake data down to the join grain before the join step rather than joining row-level profitability detail and aggregating afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: The build itself isn't the hard part — sync Opportunity and whatever related objects I need from Salesforce, bring in the Snowflake profitability table through the external connector on its own schedule, and join them in the Recipe on a shared key, usually an Account-level identifier that has to already exist on both sides; that's something I need the Snowflake/ETL team to have arranged ahead of time, not something I can conjure inside the Recipe itself. Where I'd tell the business to be careful is sync timing — if the Salesforce sync and the Snowflake sync don't run on the same schedule, this join can quietly mix today's Opportunity data with yesterday's or older profitability data, and I'd rather say that out loud upfront than have someone discover it by noticing a number doesn't match what they expected. The other real risk is the join key itself drifting — if an Account gets merged or re-keyed in Salesforce and that doesn't flow back to whatever identifier the Snowflake table is using, rows start silently failing to match with no error telling anyone it happened. And performance-wise, I wouldn't join against row-level profitability detail and then aggregate afterward if the Snowflake side is high volume — I'd aggregate it down to the Account grain before the join, because joining first and aggregating second is exactly the pattern that quietly gets slower as both tables grow.
commonMistakes: Assumes the Recipe can invent a join key between Salesforce and Snowflake without pre-existing coordination
Doesn't flag sync timing misalignment between the two sources as a real data-currency risk
Doesn't account for join key drift when Accounts are merged or re-keyed in Salesforce
Joins row-level detail first and aggregates afterward instead of aggregating before the join
Presents the blended dataset to the business without disclosing its data-currency characteristics
keyPoints: Correctly describes independent sync steps for Salesforce and Snowflake sources
Identifies the need for a pre-arranged, reliable join key across both systems
Flags sync timing misalignment as a real data-currency risk to disclose
Flags join key drift (Account merges/re-keys) as a silent failure mode
Recommends aggregating before joining for performance at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the blend build steps
Identifies realistic enterprise-scale failure points

questions.title: Writing a Cross-Object Aggregate SOQL Query for an Executive Rollup
questions.prompt: Write a SOQL query that gives an executive a count and total dollar value of closed-won Opportunities per owner for the current fiscal year, only for owners whose closed-won total exceeds $500,000, and explain a limitation of aggregate SOQL you'd flag to whoever is building the dashboard on top of this.
questions.code:
SELECT OwnerId, COUNT(Id) OppCount, SUM(Amount) TotalAmount
FROM Opportunity
WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won'
AND CloseDate = THIS_FISCAL_YEAR
GROUP BY OwnerId
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 500000
ORDER BY SUM(Amount) DESC
questions.modelAnswer: The GROUP BY OwnerId with COUNT(Id) and SUM(Amount) aggregates at the owner level in a single query, and the HAVING clause filters groups after aggregation (filtering on the aggregate SUM result itself), which is distinct from a WHERE clause that could only filter rows before aggregation and couldn't reference an aggregate function — HAVING is required here specifically because the $500,000 threshold applies to the summed total, not to any individual Opportunity's Amount. The THIS_FISCAL_YEAR date literal respects the org's configured fiscal year settings (including any fiscal year offset from the calendar year), which matters because a hardcoded calendar-year date range would silently produce the wrong result for an org on a non-calendar fiscal year, a detail that's easy to miss if you're not deliberately checking the org's fiscal settings. The real limitation I'd flag to the dashboard builder is that aggregate SOQL queries are capped at 2,000 groupings returned, and more importantly, this query has no row-level security caveat built in beyond standard sharing enforcement on the underlying Opportunity records (a query running in a context with 'without sharing' or a system context could return totals the executive isn't actually supposed to see based on org-wide defaults and sharing rules) — so whoever builds the dashboard needs to confirm the Apex or reporting layer running this query respects sharing rules appropriately for who's viewing the dashboard, because an aggregate SOQL result can easily aggregate data the viewing user wouldn't normally have individual record access to, and that's a security review point, not just a performance one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key piece here is the HAVING clause, not WHERE — the $500,000 cutoff applies to the summed total per owner, not to any single Opportunity's amount, and WHERE can't filter on an aggregate function result, only HAVING can. I used THIS_FISCAL_YEAR instead of hardcoding calendar dates specifically because this org might run on a non-calendar fiscal year with an offset, and a hardcoded date range would just quietly give a wrong answer without throwing any error. The thing I'd flag to whoever's building the actual dashboard on top of this isn't really a SOQL limitation at all, it's a security one — this kind of aggregate query can easily run in a context that bypasses normal sharing rules, and if it does, the executive dashboard could be surfacing totals that include Opportunities the viewing user wouldn't normally be able to see individually. I'd want someone to explicitly confirm the Apex running this respects sharing appropriately for whoever's looking at the dashboard, rather than assuming an aggregate number is automatically safe just because it's a sum instead of a record list.

Hardcodes a calendar-year date range instead of using THIS_FISCAL_YEAR
Doesn't flag the sharing/security implications of an aggregate query running without proper context
Assumes an aggregate SUM is inherently safe to show regardless of the viewer's record-level access
Doesn't mention the 2,000-grouping cap on aggregate SOQL results
keyPoints: Correctly uses HAVING to filter on the aggregated SUM, not WHERE
Correctly uses THIS_FISCAL_YEAR to respect the org's fiscal year configuration
Flags the sharing/security implications of aggregate queries bypassing row-level access
Understands the 2,000-grouping limit on aggregate SOQL
Distinguishes a reporting/security concern from a pure performance concern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct aggregate SOQL query with proper HAVING usage
Correctly uses fiscal-year-aware date literals
Flags a genuine, non-obvious limitation (sharing/security) to the dashboard builder

questions.title: Designing a dbt Staging/Intermediate/Mart Layering for a Salesforce Extract
questions.prompt: A Salesforce Opportunity and Account extract lands daily in Snowflake raw tables via Fivetran. Sketch the dbt model layering (staging, intermediate, marts) you'd build on top of it for a sales analytics use case, and explain specifically what business logic belongs in which layer and why getting that wrong causes problems later.
questions.modelAnswer: Staging models (stg_opportunity, stg_account) should do only mechanical transformation directly against the raw Fivetran-synced tables: renaming cryptic or inconsistent source column names to clear business names, casting types consistently (Salesforce's Amount field as a numeric type, dates cast explicitly), and light standardization like trimming whitespace — no joins, no business logic, no filtering out records based on a business rule, because the staging layer's job is to be a thin, trustworthy, one-to-one-with-source translation layer that every downstream model can rely on without re-deriving basic cleanup. Intermediate models (int_opportunities_with_account_tier, for instance) are where real business logic lives: joining Opportunity to Account, deriving fields like a deal-size tier or a sales-cycle-length calculation, and critically, this is where a single authoritative definition of something ambiguous like 'closed-won' or 'active opportunity' gets defined exactly once, rather than letting that definition drift into every downstream mart independently. Mart models (fct_opportunities, dim_accounts) are the wide, consumption-ready, one-per-business-domain tables that BI tools and dashboards actually query, built from the intermediate models, denormalized for query performance rather than normalized for storage efficiency, and should not contain net-new business logic of their own — if a mart needs new logic, that's a sign the logic belongs in the intermediate layer instead, not a reason to add it ad hoc inside the mart. Getting this wrong typically looks like business logic leaking into either staging (where it silently applies to every downstream consumer with no visibility, including ones that didn't want that filtering) or directly into marts (where it gets duplicated slightly differently across multiple marts, producing the exact 40-spreadsheets-worth-of-divergent-definitions problem a governed data platform is supposed to prevent) — the layering discipline exists specifically to create one place, the intermediate layer, where 'what does closed-won actually mean here' is decided once and inherited everywhere downstream.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep staging models completely mechanical — rename the ugly Fivetran column names to something a business user could read, cast types consistently, maybe trim some whitespace, and that's it, no joins, no business rules. The moment any real logic shows up — joining Opportunity to Account, deciding what counts as a deal-size tier, and especially nailing down one agreed definition of something like 'closed-won' — that belongs in the intermediate layer, and it belongs there exactly once, because that's the whole point: I don't want five different marts each quietly implementing their own slightly different version of what counts as a closed deal. Marts, then, are just the wide, denormalized, ready-to-query tables built on top of that intermediate logic — if I find myself wanting to add new business logic directly inside a mart, that's usually a sign I'm about to recreate the exact problem this layering is supposed to prevent, and I'd push that logic back into the intermediate layer instead. The failure mode I've actually seen is business logic sneaking into staging, where it silently applies to every single downstream consumer with zero visibility, or logic getting copy-pasted slightly differently into multiple marts — and both of those are just slower-motion versions of the forty-spreadsheets problem a governed model layer exists to kill.

Lets marts contain net-new business logic instead of only consuming intermediate models
Defines an ambiguous business term like 'closed-won' differently across multiple marts
Treats the layering as arbitrary folder organization rather than an enforcement mechanism
Doesn't explain the downstream consequence of logic leaking into the wrong layer
keyPoints: Correctly scopes staging models to mechanical, one-to-one source translation only
Correctly scopes intermediate models as the single home for real business logic
Correctly scopes marts as consumption-ready, denormalized, logic-free outputs of the intermediate layer
Explains the single-definition principle for ambiguous business terms
Explains the concrete downstream consequence of misplacing logic in the wrong layer

Correctly assigns business logic to the right layer with reasoning
Explains the real consequence of getting the layering wrong

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recursive Trigger Storm from a Flow/Apex Interaction
questions.prompt: Production reports a Case object hitting CPU timeouts sporadically, only during bulk updates. You suspect a recursion loop between an after-save Flow and an Apex trigger on the same object. Walk through your actual diagnostic process, not just your guess at the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The first diagnostic step is pulling debug logs from an actual failing bulk transaction (not reproducing in isolation with one record, since the bug is explicitly described as bulk-only) with Apex code and workflow/flow log categories both set to a high enough level to see every trigger and flow invocation within the transaction, then counting how many times the same trigger or flow context actually fires — a genuine recursion loop shows up as the same automation appearing repeatedly in one transaction's log, each iteration usually triggered by the previous one's DML on the same or a related record. The second step is identifying exactly which field update is closing the loop: if the after-save Flow updates a field on the Case that the Apex trigger's before-update or after-update logic reacts to by updating a different field, which the Flow in turn reacts to again, that's the cycle, and it only manifests as a CPU timeout under bulk load because each individual iteration is cheap but the iteration count multiplied across a large batch of records compounds quickly — a single-record manual test might complete in time even with the same underlying recursive pattern. Once the exact field-update cycle is identified, I'd check whether either side has any recursion guard at all (a static Boolean flag in Apex, or a Flow-level check on whether the field already has the target value before reupdating it) — the most common root cause is that the automation was written assuming it would only ever fire once, with no defensive check for 'is this update actually a no-op, in which case don't re-trigger the chain.' The actual fix is almost always adding an idempotency check (only perform the update if the target value would actually change) on at least one side of the cycle, which breaks the loop at its source rather than trying to out-guess the recursion with a blunt recursion-counter cutoff that just delays the timeout instead of fixing the cause.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to reproduce this with a single test record first, because the bug report itself is the clue — it's bulk-only, which almost always means it's about iteration count, not logic correctness. So I'd go straight to debug logs from an actual failing bulk transaction, with Apex and flow/workflow logging turned up enough to see every invocation, and I'd literally count how many times the same automation fires in one transaction — a real recursion loop shows up as the same trigger or flow appearing over and over, each one set off by the previous one's update. Once I can see that pattern, I'm looking for the specific field update that closes the loop — usually the Flow updates something the Apex trigger reacts to, which updates something the Flow reacts to again, and round it goes. Then I'd check whether either side even has a guard against this — more often than not, nobody put in a check for 'is this update actually a no-op,' because whoever wrote it assumed it would only fire once. And the fix I'd actually make is an idempotency check — only update the field if the new value is genuinely different from the current one — because that kills the loop at its root, instead of slapping a recursion counter on it that just pushes the timeout a little further out without fixing anything.
commonMistakes: Tries to reproduce the issue with a single test record instead of examining a real bulk transaction's logs
Doesn't count actual automation invocations in the debug log to confirm a true recursion loop
Adds a blunt recursion-counter cutoff instead of an idempotency check at the root cause
Assumes the bug is a logic error rather than an iteration-count/no-guard issue
Fixes only one side of the cycle without confirming which field update actually closes the loop
keyPoints: Diagnoses using debug logs from a real bulk transaction, not an isolated single-record test
Counts actual automation invocations to confirm a genuine recursion loop
Identifies the specific field-update cycle closing the loop
Recognizes why the issue only manifests under bulk load, not single-record testing
Fixes the loop with an idempotency/no-op check rather than a recursion-counter workaround

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Diagnoses using real bulk-transaction debug logs appropriately
Correctly identifies the recursion pattern and its bulk-only manifestation
Proposes a root-cause fix (idempotency check) over a surface workaround

questions.title: Diagnosing Too Many SOQL Queries in a Batch Apex Job at Scale
questions.prompt: A Batch Apex job that has run fine for months starts throwing 'Too many SOQL queries: 101' errors, but only on execute() invocations that process certain records, not all of them. Walk through how you'd isolate the actual cause rather than just raising the batch scope down and hoping it goes away.
questions.modelAnswer: A job that ran fine for months and suddenly fails only on certain records strongly suggests either a recent change in the data itself (a new category of record that triggers a different code path with a query inside a loop that was always there but never exercised at volume before) or a recent, possibly unrelated code change elsewhere that's now firing extra queries during the same transaction via automation on a related object, rather than a bug freshly introduced into the batch class itself — I'd check recent deployments and recent changes to related objects' automation before assuming the batch class's own code regressed. The actual isolation technique is pulling debug logs specifically for a failing execute() invocation (reproducing against the specific record subset that fails, which the error pattern tells us is identifiable) and counting SOQL statements in the log for that one execute() call, looking specifically for any query that appears once per record in the scope rather than once total — that's the signature of a query inside a loop, and it's the almost-always root cause of a '101 queries' message appearing only for certain records if those records are the ones taking a conditional branch that happens to contain the per-record query. Once the offending query is found, I'd check whether it's inside the batch class's own execute() method or inside automation (a trigger, a flow, an invocable Apex action) that the batch's DML indirectly fires on a related object — because the fix is different depending on where it lives: inside the batch class itself, it needs to move to a single bulk query built from a Set of IDs before any loop; inside downstream automation, the batch's own scope size or its DML pattern may need to change (processing in smaller sub-chunks, or restructuring to avoid triggering that automation's query-per-record pattern at all). Simply lowering the batch scope size is a mitigation that delays hitting the limit by processing fewer records per execute() call, but it doesn't fix a true per-record query pattern — it just means the failure threshold moves to a larger or smaller 'certain records' subset depending on scope, so I wouldn't present that as the actual fix, only as a stopgap while the real query-in-a-loop gets found and corrected.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that this ran fine for months and now only fails on some records tells me this probably isn't a bug freshly introduced into the batch class itself — I'd actually check recent deployments and recent changes to any automation on related objects first, because a trigger or flow that started firing an extra query per record on a related object would produce exactly this symptom without anyone touching the batch class at all. To actually isolate it, I'd pull debug logs for an execute() call that's known to fail, using the specific records that trigger it, and literally count the SOQL statements in that log — I'm looking for a query that shows up once per record instead of once for the whole execute call, because that's the fingerprint of a query sitting inside a loop. Once I find it, where it lives changes the fix — if it's inside the batch's own execute method, that's a straightforward refactor into one bulk query built from a set of IDs before the loop; if it's actually downstream automation firing on a related object because of the batch's DML, I need to fix that automation, not the batch class. And I wouldn't just drop the batch scope size and call it done — that's a stopgap that delays the failure, it doesn't actually remove a per-record query, so I'd be honest that the real fix is still pending until I find and correct that query.

Doesn't isolate debug logs to the specific failing record subset to find the per-record query
Can't distinguish a query inside the batch's own loop from a query fired by downstream automation
Doesn't recognize why the failure pattern correlates with specific records rather than all of them
keyPoints: Checks recent deployments/automation changes before assuming the batch class regressed
Isolates debug logs to a specific failing execute() invocation and counts SOQL statements
Correctly identifies a query-inside-a-loop pattern as the signature cause
Distinguishes whether the offending query lives in the batch class or in downstream automation
Treats lowering batch scope as a stopgap, not the actual fix

Correctly isolates and identifies the query-in-a-loop signature

questions.title: Diagnosing Intermittent Platform Event Delivery Failures and Replay ID Gaps
questions.prompt: An external subscriber consuming a High Volume Platform Event via the Pub/Sub API reports gaps in sequential processing — some events seem to never arrive. Walk through how you'd determine whether this is an actual platform delivery failure, a subscriber-side bug, or expected behavior you need to design around.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check is retention: Platform Events are retained on the event bus for a limited window (typically 24 hours for most event types, or longer for specific configurations), so if the subscriber was disconnected or fell behind beyond that retention window and is using a replay ID or earliest-available-position subscription, events older than the retention period are genuinely gone from the platform's perspective, not lost due to a bug — this needs to be ruled in or out first by checking the subscriber's connection/disconnection history against the event's actual publish timestamps. Second, I'd confirm whether the subscriber's replay ID handling is actually correct: a common subscriber-side bug is not persisting the last successfully processed replay ID durably before acknowledging or resuming, so a subscriber restart can either reprocess from an earlier point (producing duplicates, which is a different symptom) or, if implemented incorrectly, skip ahead past unprocessed events, which produces exactly the 'gaps' symptom described — this needs direct inspection of the subscriber's own stored replay-ID checkpoint logic, not an assumption that the platform dropped them. Third, I'd check whether the publishing side is actually guaranteed to have succeeded for the 'missing' events in the first place, by cross-referencing the EventBus.publish SaveResult list (or, if publishing via REST/Bulk API, the API response) against the specific records the subscriber claims it never received — if the publish itself silently failed for those specific records (a validation failure, exceeding a per-call limit) and nobody checked the SaveResult list on the publishing side, the events were never actually published at all, which looks identical to a 'delivery failure' from the subscriber's point of view but is actually a publishing-side bug. Only after ruling out retention-window expiry, subscriber-side replay ID mishandling, and a silent publish failure would I escalate to Salesforce as a genuine platform-side delivery issue, because all three of those are far more common root causes than an actual bus delivery failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd even consider this a platform bug, there are three much more likely explanations I'd rule out first. The first is retention — Platform Events don't live on the event bus forever, so if the subscriber was disconnected longer than the retention window, those events are genuinely gone, not lost due to any failure, and I'd check the subscriber's disconnect history against the actual publish timestamps to see if that lines up. The second is the subscriber's own replay ID handling — a really common bug is not durably saving the last successfully processed replay ID before resuming, which on a restart can cause the subscriber to skip ahead past events it never actually processed, and that looks exactly like 'gaps' from the outside even though nothing was dropped by the platform. The third, and the one people check least, is whether those events were ever actually published successfully in the first place — if whoever's publishing on the other end isn't checking the SaveResult list from EventBus.publish, a handful of records can silently fail to publish at all, and that looks identical to a delivery failure to the subscriber, when really the event never existed on the bus to begin with. Only once I've ruled out all three of those would I actually treat this as a genuine platform delivery problem and escalate it.

Doesn't inspect the subscriber's own replay ID checkpoint logic for a resume/restart bug
Doesn't check the publishing side's SaveResult list for silent publish failures
Treats 'subscriber never saw it' as proof the platform failed to deliver it
Escalates to Salesforce support before ruling out the three much more common causes
keyPoints: Checks event retention window against subscriber disconnect history first
Inspects subscriber-side replay ID persistence for a skip-ahead bug on resume
Checks the publishing side's SaveResult list for a silent publish failure
Correctly orders the investigation from most to least likely root cause
Only escalates to a genuine platform issue after ruling out the other three causes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly investigates retention window expiry first
Correctly investigates subscriber-side replay ID handling
Correctly investigates publish-side silent failures via SaveResult

questions.title: Diagnosing a Failed Unlocked Package Deployment from Dependency Ordering
questions.prompt: A 2GP unlocked package deployment fails in a downstream org with a 'required field missing' or component-not-found style error, but the exact same package version deployed cleanly in a different org last week. Walk through how you'd isolate whether this is a dependency-ordering problem, an org-specific metadata gap, or a package versioning issue.
questions.modelAnswer: The first check is whether the target org actually has every declared package dependency installed at a compatible version — a 2GP unlocked package's dependency graph is declared in its package.xml/sfdx-project.json dependency list, and if this org is missing a dependency package entirely, or has an older version of it that doesn't yet contain a field or object the installing package references, the installation can fail in a way that looks like a generic metadata error rather than clearly stating 'missing dependency,' so I'd explicitly verify installed package versions in the failing org against the manifest's declared minimum versions before looking anywhere else. Second, since the exact same package version worked in a different org, I'd compare what's different about the two orgs' existing configuration rather than assume the package itself is the variable — the most common cause here is an org-specific customization gap: the failing org might be missing a piece of base, unpackaged metadata the package assumes exists (a specific record type, a permission set, a custom field the package's Apex or validation rules reference that isn't itself part of the package, often because it was manually created in the working org rather than packaged), which is exactly the kind of gap that org-dependent packaging would mask differently than true 2GP unlocked packaging, which should fail loudly here rather than silently accepting a missing reference. Third, if dependencies all check out and base metadata genuinely matches between the two orgs, I'd check whether there's an installation-order issue within this single deployment itself — if multiple packages or a package plus loose metadata are being installed together and this org's deployment pipeline doesn't guarantee the same install order as the working org's pipeline did, a package that depends on another package's metadata being present first can fail if it happens to install before its dependency in this particular run. Isolating between these three means checking installed package versions first (fastest, most common cause), then diffing org-specific unpackaged metadata second, then auditing the deployment pipeline's install-order logic third — and I would not accept the generic error message at face value as telling me which of the three it is, since 2GP error messages for missing dependencies and missing org metadata often look similar.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since the exact same package version worked somewhere else, my instinct is that the package itself probably isn't the broken variable here — something about this specific org is. So first I'd check installed package versions in the failing org against what this package's manifest actually declares as its minimum dependency versions, because a missing or outdated dependency package can throw an error that doesn't clearly say 'you're missing a dependency,' it just says a field or component wasn't found. If that checks out, I'd compare the two orgs' own unpackaged metadata, because the most common real-world cause of 'works here, fails there' with the identical package version is that the working org happened to already have some piece of base configuration — a record type, a permission set, a referenced custom field — that somebody created manually in that org and never packaged, and the failing org just doesn't have it. And if both of those check out, I'd look at install order within this specific deployment — if this org's pipeline is installing multiple packages or loose metadata in a different sequence than the working org did, something that depends on another piece being installed first can fail purely because of ordering, even with an identical package version. I wouldn't trust the generic error message to tell me which of those three it is on its own — I've seen a missing-dependency error and a missing-org-metadata error look nearly identical.

questions.title: Diagnosing Degraded LWC Record-Page Performance from Excessive Wire Re-Renders
questions.prompt: Users report a record page feels noticeably slower after a new LWC component was added, with visible lag on every field edit, not just on page load. Walk through how you'd confirm whether excessive wire service re-renders are the cause before touching any code.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the lag happens on every field edit, not just initial load, the first thing to check is whether the new component is wired to getRecord or a custom Apex wire using a reactive parameter that's broader than it needs to be — if the wire is scoped to the whole record (all fields) rather than the specific fields the component actually renders, any field edit anywhere on the page re-triggers Lightning Data Service's cache invalidation and a re-fetch for every component wired that broadly, even ones that don't display the edited field, which produces exactly this 'lag on every edit' symptom. I'd confirm this using the browser's performance/network tooling (or the Lightning component performance panel) during a field edit specifically, watching for repeated Apex or getRecord wire invocations firing in response to a single field save, and cross-referencing timestamps against which components on the page re-render in that window — if the new component's wire fires on every edit regardless of which field changed, that confirms over-broad field scoping as the mechanism, not just a correlation with when the component was added. Second, I'd check whether the new component is doing anything inside its wire's reactive callback or a connected lifecycle hook that's expensive per re-render (a loop over a large dataset, DOM manipulation outside the framework's reactivity, a synchronous Apex call not marked cacheable), since a narrowly-scoped wire that still re-renders expensively is a different problem with a different fix than an over-broadly-scoped wire. Only after confirming which of these two (or both) is actually happening would I change code — the fix for over-broad field scoping is narrowing the getRecord fields array or the Apex wire's parameters to exactly what's rendered, while the fix for expensive re-render logic is moving that work out of the hot path or memoizing it, and conflating the two leads to fixing the wrong thing first.
questions.professionalAnswer: Because the lag happens on every single field edit, not just when the page first loads, that's actually a pretty specific clue — it points at the wire service re-fetching more than it needs to on every change, not at a one-time slow load. So before I touch any code, I'd check what fields the new component's wire is actually scoped to — if it's wired to getRecord with every field, or a custom Apex wire with a broad reactive parameter, then literally any field edit anywhere on that page invalidates the cache and re-fetches for that component, even if the edited field has nothing to do with what it displays. I'd confirm that with the browser's network or performance tooling while actually editing an unrelated field, watching whether the new component's wire fires anyway — if it does every time regardless of which field changed, that's the smoking gun, not just a coincidence of timing with when the component got added. I'd also separately check whether the component's own re-render logic is doing something expensive — looping over a big dataset, manual DOM work, a non-cacheable Apex call — because that's a different problem with a different fix, and if I don't tell those two apart first, I might narrow the wire's field scope, feel good about it, and still have the real expensive-re-render problem sitting there untouched.

questions.title: Diagnosing OAuth JWT Bearer Flow Failures from Certificate/Consumer Key Mismatches
questions.prompt: A nightly integration using the JWT Bearer OAuth flow suddenly starts failing with an 'invalid_grant' or similar authentication error after working for months with no code changes. Walk through your diagnostic sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Since nothing in the code changed, the first and most common cause to check is certificate expiration: the JWT is signed with a private key whose corresponding public certificate is uploaded to the Connected App, and that certificate has an expiration date — if it quietly expired, the JWT's signature verification fails, producing exactly an invalid_grant-style error with no code-level change required to trigger it, so checking the certificate's expiration date against today's date is the fastest, highest-probability first check. Second, I'd verify the Connected App configuration itself hasn't changed independent of the integration's code: a Connected App being deactivated, the pre-authorized user being deactivated or losing the required permission set/profile access, or an admin rotating the certificate on the Connected App side without coordinating with whoever maintains the integration's signing key, are all org-administration changes that would produce this exact symptom with zero code changes on the integration side. Third, I'd check the JWT's claims themselves for a clock-skew or expiration issue — the JWT's exp claim needs to be within a tight window of actual current time (JWT Bearer tokens are typically valid for only a few minutes), so if the server generating the JWT has a misconfigured system clock (common after an OS update or a VM host issue) that's drifted significantly, the token can appear expired to Salesforce's servers even though it was 'just' generated, which again requires no code change to start failing. Fourth, I'd confirm the username being asserted in the JWT still exists, is active, and still has API access enabled, since a user deactivation or a profile change removing API access produces the same generic auth failure. I'd check these in order of probability (certificate expiration first, Connected App/user admin changes second, clock skew third, user status fourth) rather than assuming a code regression, because the 'no code changes' detail is the strongest signal that this is an external, time-based, or administrative change, not a logic bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that nothing in the code changed is actually the most useful clue here, because it points away from a logic bug and toward something time-based or administrative. So my first check, every time, is certificate expiration — the JWT gets signed with a private key whose public cert lives on the Connected App, and if that cert quietly expired, the signature check fails with exactly this kind of generic invalid_grant error, with zero code changes needed to trigger it. If the cert's fine, I'd check whether anything changed on the admin side independent of the integration code — did the Connected App get deactivated, did the pre-authorized integration user lose a permission set or get deactivated, did someone rotate the certificate on the Salesforce side without telling whoever maintains the signing key on our end. Next I'd check clock skew on the server generating the JWT — these tokens are only valid for a few minutes, so if that server's clock drifted, even a 'freshly generated' token can look expired by the time Salesforce checks it, and that's the kind of thing an OS update or a VM host hiccup causes without anyone touching a line of code. And finally I'd just confirm the asserted username is still active with API access, since a deactivation produces the same generic failure. I'd go through those in that order, because the probability is heavily weighted toward 'something expired or got changed on the admin side,' not 'the code broke itself.'

Doesn't check certificate expiration as the first, highest-probability cause
Doesn't consider administrative changes (Connected App, user deactivation) independent of code
Doesn't consider clock skew on the JWT-generating server as a cause of apparent token expiration
Doesn't verify the asserted username's active status and API access

Checks certificate expiration first as the most probable cause

questions.title: Diagnosing a CPU Timeout in a Synchronous Apex Transaction from a Lightning Action
questions.prompt: A Lightning quick action that calls synchronous Apex intermittently throws a CPU time limit exceeded error, but only for a subset of users, and only at certain times of day. Walk through how you'd isolate the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The 'only certain users, only certain times of day' pattern is the key clue, and it points toward data-dependent or load-dependent CPU cost rather than a uniform logic bug, so the first check is whether the affected users share something about the records they're acting on — larger accounts with more related child records, deeper role hierarchies, more complex sharing rule evaluation, or simply being in a time zone whose working hours overlap with a nightly batch job or another high-volume process competing for the same CPU-bound resources at those specific times. I'd pull debug logs specifically from a failing invocation for one of the affected users (not a synthetic reproduction with sanitized test data, since the failure is explicitly data- and timing-dependent) and look at the CPU time breakdown across the transaction, specifically checking whether the cost is dominated by the Lightning action's own Apex logic, by automation triggered indirectly through its DML (another trigger, workflow, or flow on records it updates), or by sharing recalculation cost triggered by the update itself — all three show up as 'CPU time exceeded' but have very different fixes. If the affected users correlate with larger or more complex Account/Opportunity hierarchies, that points to the Apex logic (or triggered automation) doing work that scales with related-record count without being capped or optimized — a classic example being a loop that walks an unbounded number of related records inline during the transaction. If the failures correlate with time of day rather than user/data characteristics, that points to CPU contention from a concurrent batch or integration process rather than the quick action's own logic being inherently too expensive, in which case the fix is scheduling that batch process outside business hours or reducing its CPU footprint, not optimizing the Lightning action itself. I'd resist jumping to 'move it to async Apex' as a default fix before this diagnosis, because async Apex has its own, different CPU limit and moving a transaction async doesn't fix an underlying O(n) pattern that scales with data size — it just changes which limit eventually gets hit as data grows further.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd lean on hardest is that this only hits certain users at certain times — that's not what a flat-out logic bug usually looks like, that's what a cost-that-scales-with-something looks like. So first I'd check whether the affected users have something in common about the data they're touching — bigger accounts, deeper hierarchies, more related records — because if the Apex logic or anything it triggers scales with related-record count, that would explain why it's user-specific. I'd pull debug logs from an actual failing invocation for one of those users, not a clean synthetic test, and look at where the CPU time is actually going — is it the action's own code, is it automation that fires because of its DML, or is it sharing recalculation kicked off by the update — because those three look identical from the error message alone but need completely different fixes. If it really does track with time of day more than with which user or which data, then I'd stop looking at the Lightning action's own code entirely and go look at what batch job or integration process runs around that time competing for the same CPU-bound resources — the fix there is rescheduling that other process, not touching this one. And I'd specifically avoid just throwing this into async Apex as a quick fix before I've done that diagnosis, because async Apex has its own CPU ceiling too — if there's a real unbounded-growth pattern in the logic, moving it async just buys time before the exact same problem shows up again as data keeps growing.
commonMistakes: Treats the error as a uniform logic bug rather than investigating the user/time correlation
Reproduces with sanitized test data instead of examining logs from an actual failing invocation
Doesn't distinguish CPU cost from the action's own logic vs. triggered automation vs. sharing recalculation
Jumps straight to moving the transaction to async Apex without diagnosing the root cause
Doesn't consider CPU contention from a concurrent batch/integration process at specific times
keyPoints: Correctly reads the user/time correlation as a clue pointing to data- or load-dependent cost
Uses debug logs from an actual failing invocation, not a sanitized reproduction
Distinguishes the three possible CPU cost sources (own logic, triggered automation, sharing recalc)
Considers CPU contention from a concurrent process correlated with time of day
Avoids defaulting to async Apex as a fix without diagnosing the underlying pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about the user/time correlation as a diagnostic clue
Correctly distinguishes the possible sources of CPU cost
Avoids a default 'move to async' fix without root-cause diagnosis

questions.title: Diagnosing Hours-Long Sharing Recalculation After a Role Hierarchy Change
questions.prompt: A role hierarchy change on a 10-million-row org triggers a sharing recalculation job that's still running six hours later, well past when the business expected it to finish, and users are reporting stale access during that window. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether this is expected behavior at this scale, a data skew problem, or a misconfiguration.
questions.modelAnswer: The first check is whether the role being moved (or the role hierarchy position being changed) has ownership skew — if a disproportionate number of records are owned by users under that specific role, the recalculation job's duration is directly proportional to how many records need their sharing reassessed, so six hours on 10 million total rows might be entirely expected if the moved role sits above a very large number of owned records, versus genuinely anomalous if the role in question only owns a modest fraction of the org's data. I'd check this concretely by querying record ownership counts grouped by the affected role (or the users under it) before assuming either 'this is normal at our scale' or 'something is misconfigured' — that number directly predicts expected recalculation duration far better than total org row count alone does. Second, I'd check whether the org has deferred sharing calculation available and whether it was used for this change — if an admin made the role hierarchy change directly rather than through a planned process that defers recalculation, performs the hierarchy change, and then triggers one explicit recalculation, the default behavior recalculates sharing synchronously as part of the triggering change in a way that's both slower and gives you less visibility into progress than a deliberately deferred, monitored recalculation job would. Third, I'd check whether overly broad sharing rules (role-and-subordinates sharing rules, or criteria-based sharing rules with broad criteria) on the affected object are contributing to recalculation scope beyond what's strictly necessary for this specific role change — a sharing rule that's broader than the business actually needs increases the blast radius of every single role hierarchy change going forward, not just this one, so if the recalculation genuinely is disproportionate to the data actually affected, overly broad sharing rule scope is a common root cause worth auditing. I'd present 'six hours' to the business as either expected (if ownership skew under that role is genuinely large) or a real problem worth fixing (if it isn't), rather than assuming either answer without actually checking record counts first.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I tell anyone whether six hours is normal or broken, I need one number: how many records are actually owned under that specific role that moved. If that role sits above a genuinely huge chunk of the org's 10 million rows, six hours might be completely expected — the recalculation job's duration tracks with how many records need reassessing, not with the org's total size. If it's a modest fraction, then six hours is a real problem and I'd keep digging. Next I'd check whether this change went through a deliberate deferred-recalculation process or was just made directly in the UI — making a role hierarchy change directly triggers a synchronous recalculation with no real visibility into progress, versus a planned process that defers recalculation, makes the change, and kicks off one explicit, monitored job, which is both faster to reason about and gives the business an actual ETA instead of 'we're not sure when this finishes.' And I'd specifically audit the sharing rules on the affected object for anything broader than it needs to be — a role-and-subordinates or criteria-based sharing rule with wide criteria increases the blast radius of every single role change from now on, not just this one, so if this really is disproportionate to the actual record count affected, an overly broad sharing rule is my top suspect.
commonMistakes: Assumes six hours is either automatically normal or automatically broken without checking record ownership counts
Doesn't check whether the role hierarchy change was made through a deferred-recalculation process
Doesn't audit sharing rule scope (role-and-subordinates, broad criteria-based rules) as a contributing factor
Uses total org row count as the benchmark instead of records owned under the specific affected role
Treats the recalculation duration as purely a platform performance issue with no actionable root cause
keyPoints: Checks record ownership counts under the specific affected role as the key diagnostic number
Checks whether a deferred-recalculation process was used for the change
Audits sharing rule scope as a contributing factor to recalculation blast radius
Uses role-specific ownership count, not total org size, as the relevant benchmark
Gives the business an accurate expected-vs-anomalous assessment based on real data, not assumption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies role-specific ownership count as the key diagnostic
Checks for deferred-recalculation process usage
Audits sharing rule scope as a contributing factor
Gives an evidence-based, not assumed, normal-vs-anomalous assessment

questions.title: Diagnosing a Failing Bulk API Load from Row Lock Contention
questions.prompt: A nightly Bulk API load of 500,000 records into a custom object fails a meaningful percentage of rows with row-lock-related errors, but only when run concurrently with another scheduled job that updates a related parent object. Walk through how you'd confirm lock contention as the cause and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: The first confirmation step is checking the specific error text in the failedResults for the affected rows — a genuine row lock contention failure in Salesforce surfaces as an UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW error, which is distinct from a validation or data-quality failure, so confirming that's the actual error code rather than assuming it from the timing correlation alone is the necessary first step before designing a fix around locking specifically. Second, I'd confirm the mechanism: if the custom object being bulk-loaded has a master-detail relationship to the parent object the other scheduled job is updating, Salesforce locks the parent record (and, depending on the relationship and sharing model, can extend locking behavior to sibling child records under the same parent) during certain parent-side DML operations, so two processes touching records under the same or related parents concurrently can legitimately contend for the same row locks — I'd check whether the failing rows cluster under a specific subset of parent records that the other job happens to be touching at the same time, which would confirm the shared-parent locking mechanism rather than a coincidental correlation. Third, once confirmed, the fix options are: reschedule the two jobs to not overlap at all (the simplest fix if there's no hard business requirement for both to run concurrently), reduce the Bulk API job's concurrency mode (Bulk API 2.0 and 1.0 both support serial processing mode for an ingest job, trading throughput for reduced lock contention, which is a reasonable tradeoff for a nightly batch window with slack time), or, if the two processes genuinely must run concurrently for a business reason, redesign the parent-update job to batch and commit its changes to the specific parent records it needs to touch in smaller, faster transactions rather than one long-held lock window, reducing the overlap window during which contention can occur. I would not recommend simply retrying failed rows blindly as the long-term fix, since that just resubmits into the same contention window on the next scheduled run without addressing why the contention exists.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd actually verify, not assume, is the exact error code on the failed rows — an UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW error specifically confirms this is a locking issue, as opposed to some other failure that just happens to correlate with timing. Once I've confirmed that, I'd check whether the object I'm bulk-loading has a master-detail relationship to that parent object the other job is updating, because Salesforce locks parent records — and depending on the relationship, can extend that to related child records — during certain updates, so two jobs touching records under the same parents at the same time can genuinely collide. I'd look at whether the failing rows cluster under the specific parents that other job happens to be touching right then, which would confirm it's really the shared-parent locking mechanism and not just a coincidence of timing. For the actual fix, the simplest option is just not running the two jobs at the same time if there's no real reason they both need to — that alone probably solves it. If they do need to overlap, I'd look at running the Bulk API job in serial mode instead of parallel, trading some throughput for a lot less contention, which is usually a fine tradeoff in an overnight batch window. And if both of those are off the table for some business reason, I'd push the other job to commit its parent-record updates in smaller, faster transactions instead of one long-held lock, so the actual window where contention can happen shrinks. What I wouldn't do is just retry the failed rows and call it done, because that's resubmitting into the exact same contention window next time this runs.
commonMistakes: Assumes lock contention from the timing correlation alone without confirming the actual error code
Doesn't check whether the failing rows cluster under the specific parents the other job touches
Treats blind retry of failed rows as an acceptable long-term fix
Doesn't consider rescheduling or serial-mode processing as simpler fixes before a redesign
Doesn't understand the master-detail parent-locking mechanism behind row lock contention
keyPoints: Confirms UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW as the actual error before assuming lock contention
Confirms the shared-parent locking mechanism by checking which parents the failing rows cluster under
Proposes rescheduling or serial-mode processing as the simplest fixes first
Proposes redesigning transaction size/duration if concurrent execution is a hard requirement
Avoids blind retry as a substitute for addressing the root cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly confirms the lock contention error and mechanism
Proposes correct, prioritized fixes (reschedule, serial mode, redesign)
Avoids treating blind retry as an acceptable long-term fix

questions.title: Diagnosing Stale or Incorrect Data in a CRM Analytics Dataset After a Dataflow Change
questions.prompt: An executive dashboard built on CRM Analytics starts showing numbers that don't match the underlying Salesforce reports, right after a data engineer modified the Dataflow feeding the dataset. Walk through how you'd isolate exactly where the discrepancy was introduced.
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is confirming the timing correlation is actually causal, not coincidental, by checking the Dataflow's run history and comparing the dataset's last successful run timestamp against when the discrepancy was first reported — if there's a Data Sync or Dataflow run that failed or ran with errors around that time, the dataset might be serving a stale snapshot from before the change rather than reflecting the new (possibly also broken) logic, which is a different problem than a logic bug in the new transformation. Second, assuming the Dataflow did run successfully with the new logic, I'd isolate the specific node the data engineer changed and manually trace a handful of known records through it — picking a few real Account or Opportunity records where the Salesforce report and the dashboard now disagree, and checking what that record's values look like at each stage of the Dataflow (before the changed node, immediately after it, and at the final dataset output), which pinpoints whether the discrepancy is introduced exactly at the changed node or somewhere else entirely that just happens to be downstream of it. Third, I'd specifically check whether the changed node altered a filter, an aggregation grain, or a join condition in a way that changes which records are included or how they're grouped, since the most common cause of 'dashboard total doesn't match report total' after a Dataflow change is a shift in grain or filter scope (the report counts at the Opportunity level, the dataset's new transform rolled up to Account level with a different aggregation rule, for instance) rather than a value being computed incorrectly per se. Fourth, once the specific discrepancy is isolated to a node and a mechanism, I'd check whether it was reviewed and tested against a known-good sample before being deployed, and if not, treat that as the actual process gap to fix going forward — testing a Dataflow/Recipe change against a reconciliation check (comparing a sample of known values against the Salesforce source before shipping) should be a standard step, not an afterthought discovered only after the business notices wrong numbers on an executive dashboard.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I even look at the new transformation logic, I'd check whether the dataset's last successful run actually happened after the change, or whether something failed and the dashboard is quietly serving an old snapshot — because 'stale data' and 'wrong new logic' are two completely different problems with the same symptom, and I don't want to debug the wrong one. Assuming the Dataflow did run clean with the new logic, I'd pick a handful of real records where the report and dashboard disagree and trace them through the Dataflow step by step — what did this record look like right before the node that got changed, right after it, and at the final dataset — because that tells me definitively whether the discrepancy actually starts at the changed node or somewhere else that just happens to sit downstream of it. My first suspicion for the mechanism itself would be a shift in filter scope or aggregation grain, not a flat-out wrong calculation — 'dashboard total doesn't match report total' after a transform change is very often the report counting at one grain and the new transform now rolling up at a different one, rather than any single number being computed incorrectly. And once I've actually found it, the bigger fix I'd push for is process, not just this one bug — if this change went out without being checked against a reconciliation sample first, that's the real gap, and I'd rather build that check in going forward than keep catching these after an executive has already noticed.
commonMistakes: Assumes the new transformation logic is wrong without first ruling out a stale/failed run
Doesn't trace specific known records step-by-step through the Dataflow to isolate the exact node
Assumes a value-calculation bug without first checking for a grain/filter-scope shift
Doesn't identify or propose a reconciliation-testing process gap as the underlying issue
Treats this as a one-off bug fix rather than identifying a repeatable verification step for future changes
keyPoints: Rules out a stale/failed run before assuming the new logic itself is wrong
Traces specific known records through the Dataflow to isolate the exact discrepancy point
Checks for a grain/filter-scope shift as a likely mechanism, not just a value-calculation error
Identifies the missing reconciliation-testing step as the real process gap
Proposes a repeatable verification process for future Dataflow/Recipe changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out a stale/failed run before blaming the new logic
Correctly traces and isolates the discrepancy to a specific node/mechanism
Correctly identifies grain/filter-scope shift as a likely mechanism
Proposes a process fix (reconciliation testing), not just a one-off patch

questions.title: Diagnosing a Broken dbt Incremental Model After a Salesforce Schema Change
questions.prompt: A dbt incremental model that transforms synced Salesforce Opportunity data starts silently producing incomplete results after an admin added a new picklist value to the StageName field in Salesforce. Walk through how an incremental materialization strategy can break this way, and how you'd both fix it and prevent a recurrence.
questions.modelAnswer: An incremental model only processes new or changed rows since its last run, typically based on a timestamp or an is_incremental() filter condition, and it does not automatically re-evaluate any hardcoded business logic that was written assuming a fixed, known set of picklist values — if the model (or, more likely, logic in the intermediate layer feeding it) contains a CASE statement or a filter that explicitly lists out known StageName values rather than handling an 'any other value' branch generically, a new picklist value added in Salesforce falls through with no matching branch, often silently producing a null or being excluded from a filter condition entirely rather than throwing a visible error, which is exactly the kind of failure that doesn't announce itself. The reason this is specifically dangerous in an incremental model, more than a full-refresh model, is that a full-refresh model re-evaluates and would immediately make the gap in output visible across the entire dataset the next time anyone looked at historical totals, whereas an incremental model only affects rows loaded after the schema change, so historical data still looks correct and the problem shows up as a slow, partial degradation in new records only, which is much easier to miss until someone specifically investigates recent data. The immediate fix is a full-refresh run of the affected model (dbt's --full-refresh flag) to reprocess all historical data with corrected logic, paired with fixing the actual CASE/filter logic to either handle the new picklist value explicitly or, better, replace an exhaustive value-by-value listing with a more defensive pattern (an explicit else/default branch that flags or logs unrecognized values rather than silently excluding them, or querying a Salesforce-side picklist metadata reference instead of hardcoding values in SQL). For prevention, I'd add a dbt test (a singular test or an accepted_values-style generic test, inverted to alert on unexpected rather than only validate expected values) that fails the build the moment an un-mapped StageName value appears in the source data, so the next time an admin adds a picklist value, CI catches it immediately instead of the gap silently accumulating in production for however long it takes someone to notice.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem is that an incremental model only touches new or changed rows going forward — it doesn't automatically go back and re-check old business logic against new data — so if there's a CASE statement somewhere, probably in the intermediate layer, that explicitly lists out known StageName values instead of handling 'anything else' generically, a new picklist value just falls through with no matching branch. And the reason that's nastier in an incremental model specifically is that it doesn't announce itself the way a full-refresh model would — historical data still looks completely fine, it's only new records from here forward that are quietly wrong, which is exactly the kind of degradation that can run for weeks before someone notices numbers feel a little off. To fix it, I'd run a full refresh to reprocess everything with corrected logic, and fix the actual CASE statement to either explicitly handle the new value or, better, stop hardcoding an exhaustive list of values at all and add a real default branch that flags anything unrecognized instead of silently dropping it. But the fix I'd actually care more about is prevention — I'd add a dbt test that fails the build the moment it sees a StageName value that isn't in the mapped set, so the next time someone adds a picklist value in Salesforce, CI catches it that same day instead of this exact silent-degradation pattern happening again.
