Fixes only the current data without running a full refresh to correct historical gaps
Replaces the hardcoded value list with another hardcoded list instead of a defensive default branch
Doesn't add a test to catch future unmapped values before they silently degrade production data again
Assumes the failure would be visible/loud rather than a silent, partial degradation
keyPoints: Correctly explains why an incremental model hides this failure as a silent, partial degradation
Runs a full refresh to correct historical data after fixing the logic
Replaces exhaustive hardcoded value matching with a defensive default/flagging branch
Adds a dbt test to catch future unmapped picklist values before they reach production silently
Distinguishes why this is more dangerous in incremental models than full-refresh models

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the incremental-model failure mechanism
Proposes a correct immediate fix (full refresh plus defensive logic)
Proposes a concrete test-based prevention mechanism

questions.title: Diagnosing Missing Records in an Airflow-Orchestrated Salesforce-to-Snowflake Pipeline
questions.prompt: A daily Airflow DAG extracts Opportunity records from Salesforce via the Bulk API and loads them into Snowflake. For the past week, the Snowflake table has been missing a small, inconsistent number of records each day compared to Salesforce. Walk through your diagnostic sequence across the pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check, before assuming a pipeline bug, is whether the extraction query itself has a selectivity or timing boundary issue — a common cause of a small, inconsistent daily record gap is an extraction filter based on a LastModifiedDate or SystemModstamp window that doesn't account for records modified very close to the extraction window's boundary (a record updated at 11:59:58 PM might fall into tomorrow's window instead of today's, or vice versa, depending on exact boundary handling and time zone normalization between Salesforce's UTC timestamps and the DAG's scheduling time zone), which would explain why the gap is small and inconsistent rather than a large, consistent failure. Second, I'd check the Airflow task logs for the specific Bulk API job's result, not just whether the DAG task reported success — exactly like the hands-on Bulk API error-handling pattern, a Bulk API job can report overall success while containing individual row-level failures in its failedResults, so if the DAG's extraction task only checks the job's overall completion status and never inspects failedResults, a small number of per-record extraction failures would be silently dropped with the DAG reporting green every day. Third, I'd check the load side into Snowflake for silent row-level rejection — if the load step has any data validation, a staging table constraint, or a deduplication/merge step with a join key that doesn't always match (a null or malformed ID on a small number of records), those specific rows could be silently excluded during the load rather than the extraction, and the way to distinguish this from an extraction-side gap is checking whether the missing records exist in the raw extracted file/staging table before the final load step, or whether they were missing even from that first intermediate output. Fourth, I'd check for a timing race between the extraction window and when Salesforce data becomes fully consistent after a bulk operation, since Bulk API queries against very recently created or modified records can occasionally be affected by indexing or replication timing in a way that a tight extraction window run very soon after business hours could miss a handful of just-committed records. I'd isolate between these four by checking, in order: the extraction filter's boundary logic, the Bulk API job's failedResults, the staging/raw data before the final load step, and finally extraction timing relative to Salesforce write completion — because each produces the same 'small, inconsistent daily gap' symptom but has a completely different fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since this is a small, inconsistent gap rather than a big obvious failure, I'd start by looking really closely at the extraction filter's time boundary — a lot of these show up because the extraction window is based on a last-modified timestamp and doesn't handle records modified right at the edge of that window cleanly, especially once you factor in Salesforce's UTC timestamps versus whatever time zone the DAG is scheduled in. Next, I'd actually open the Bulk API job's results for a few of the affected days, not just check whether the Airflow task says success, because a Bulk API job can report overall success while still having individual rows fail in its failedResults — if the extraction task never checks that file, a handful of per-record failures disappear completely with the DAG looking green every single day. Then I'd check the load side into Snowflake separately — if there's any validation, constraint, or merge step with a join key that doesn't always match cleanly, a few rows could get silently dropped there instead, and I'd tell the difference by checking whether the missing records ever even made it into the raw staging table before the final load. And finally, I'd consider timing — if this extraction runs very soon after business hours, there's a chance a just-written record hasn't fully settled yet when the Bulk API query runs. I'd check those four in that order, because they all look identical from the outside — 'a few records missing every day' — but each one needs a completely different fix.
commonMistakes: Assumes a pipeline code bug without first checking the extraction filter's time-boundary logic
Only checks the Airflow task's overall success status instead of the Bulk API job's failedResults
Doesn't distinguish an extraction-side gap from a load-side silent rejection in Snowflake
Doesn't consider timing/consistency issues between extraction and recent Salesforce writes
Treats the inconsistent, small gap as random noise rather than systematically isolating its source
keyPoints: Checks the extraction filter's time-boundary/time-zone handling as a likely cause
Explicitly checks Bulk API failedResults, not just overall job/task success
Distinguishes an extraction-side gap from a load-side silent rejection by checking staging data
Considers timing/consistency race conditions between extraction and recent writes
Systematically isolates among multiple plausible causes rather than guessing at one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks extraction filter boundary logic as a likely cause
Checks Bulk API failedResults rather than trusting overall job status
Distinguishes extraction-side vs. load-side silent data loss
Considers timing/consistency race conditions

questions.title: Diagnosing a Data Governance Incident: PII in a Non-Compliant Sandbox Refresh
questions.prompt: A partial-copy sandbox refresh over the weekend pulled live customer PII (SSNs, in an unmasked custom field) into an environment accessible to 40 contractors with broad sandbox access, violating the org's data governance policy. Walk through how you'd diagnose the scope of exposure and what you'd do in the first 24 hours.
questions.modelAnswer: The first diagnostic step is confirming exactly what was actually exposed and for how long: checking the sandbox refresh logs to confirm the refresh timestamp, checking whether Data Mask (Salesforce's native masking tool) or an equivalent masking step was supposed to run as part of this environment's refresh process and why it didn't (a disabled scheduled mask job, a masking policy that doesn't cover this specific custom field because it was added after the masking policy was last configured, or a refresh type that bypassed the masking step entirely), and checking login/access logs for that sandbox across the exposure window to determine which of the 40 contractors actually accessed records containing the field in question, rather than assuming all 40 saw it just because they had access. Second, within the first 24 hours, the immediate containment action is restricting or revoking sandbox access for anyone who didn't have a legitimate, already-in-progress need to be in that environment, and either re-masking the field immediately (running Data Mask against just this sandbox now, which doesn't undo exposure that already happened but stops ongoing exposure) or restricting field-level access to that field via a permission set change if a full re-mask takes longer to execute than is acceptable for the exposure window. Third, this needs to be escalated to whoever owns data governance and compliance (not handled as a quiet, technical-only fix) within the first 24 hours, because unmasked SSN exposure to that many users for that long is very likely a reportable incident under whatever regulatory framework applies (depending on jurisdiction and industry, this could trigger breach notification obligations), and that determination needs to be made by the compliance/legal function with accurate technical facts from the investigation, not assumed away by engineering. Fourth, the root-cause fix beyond this single incident is auditing the masking policy configuration itself to confirm every sensitive field across every object is covered by the standing masking policy (not just the fields that existed when the policy was first configured), and adding a verification gate to the sandbox refresh process itself that confirms masking completed successfully before the refreshed sandbox is made accessible, rather than trusting it ran correctly after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I need, before I can tell anyone how bad this actually is, is the real scope — I'd check the refresh logs for the exact timestamp, check why Data Mask didn't cover this field (did the masking policy just never get updated after this custom field was added, was there a scheduled mask job that's disabled, did this refresh type skip masking entirely), and check access logs across the exposure window to see who actually opened records with that field, not just assume all 40 contractors saw it because they technically had access. In the first 24 hours, containment comes first — cut sandbox access down to only people with a genuine active need, and either re-mask that field right now or, if a full mask run takes too long, lock down field-level access on it with a permission set change in the meantime, understanding that neither of those undoes exposure that's already happened, they just stop it from continuing. And I would not try to handle this quietly as a pure engineering fix — unmasked SSNs exposed to that many people for that long is exactly the kind of thing that needs to go to whoever owns compliance and legal immediately, because whether this is a reportable incident is their call to make, with accurate facts from me, not something I get to decide is 'probably fine' on my own. After the immediate response, the real fix is auditing the masking policy itself to make sure every sensitive field, including ones added after the policy was last touched, is actually covered, and adding a hard check into the refresh process that verifies masking actually completed before anyone gets access to the refreshed sandbox — not just trusting that it ran.
commonMistakes: Assumes all 40 contractors saw the exposed data without checking actual access logs
Treats this as a purely technical fix without escalating to compliance/legal for a breach determination
Doesn't investigate why the masking policy failed to cover this specific field

questions.title: System Design: Collapsing a 14-Org Conglomerate onto One Governed Salesforce Platform
questions.prompt: A conglomerate formed through a decade of acquisitions runs 14 separate Salesforce orgs across its business units, each with its own data model, automation, and integrations. The board wants one consolidated platform within 18 months to enable cross-sell reporting and shared customer service, without disrupting any business unit's ability to close deals during the transition. Design the technical architecture and migration strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture decision is not 'one org' as a foregone conclusion — it's determining which of the 14 orgs' differences are genuine business-model differences that justify separation (a regulated subsidiary with different compliance obligations, a business unit with a fundamentally different sales process and object model) versus which are just historical accidents of having been acquired separately with no real reason to stay apart, and consolidating only the latter onto one platform while deliberately keeping the former separate with a thin integration layer connecting them for the cross-sell reporting requirement. For the units that do consolidate, the data model needs a canonical design built from the actual requirement (cross-sell visibility and shared service, which needs a unified Account/Contact model and a shared Case/Service model) rather than attempting to merge all 14 units' existing custom objects wholesale, which would import a decade of accumulated technical debt into the new platform. Migration itself needs to be staged by business unit, not attempted as a single cutover, specifically because the requirement that no unit can lose deal-closing capability during the transition means each unit's migration needs its own rehearsed cutover window, validated data reconciliation, and rollback plan, and running 14 of those sequentially (or in small parallel batches where units don't share dependencies) is the only way to keep the blast radius of any single migration's problems contained to one business unit rather than the whole platform. I'd also use this as the natural forcing function to retire shadow automation and legacy customizations that have no real audit trail, since a decade of 14 separately-evolved orgs guarantees meaningful amounts of undocumented, unowned automation that shouldn't simply be ported forward as-is.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start this project by assuming 'one org' is the answer — the first six weeks of this, for me, is figuring out which of these 14 are different for a real business reason, like a regulated subsidiary or a genuinely different sales motion, versus which are different purely because they got acquired separately and nobody ever had a reason to merge them. The ones with a real reason to stay separate, I'd keep separate, and connect them to the consolidated platform with a thin integration layer just for the cross-sell and shared-service requirement the board actually asked for. For the ones that do consolidate, I'm not trying to merge fourteen different custom object models together — I'm designing one canonical Account, Contact, and Case model from what the business actually needs, and migrating each unit's data into that, not importing a decade of accumulated workarounds as-is. And I'd never attempt this as one big-bang cutover across all fourteen — each business unit gets its own staged migration with its own rehearsed cutover and rollback plan, because the one thing the board explicitly cannot have is any single unit losing its ability to close deals, and that only holds if a bad migration in one unit can't take down the others.
commonMistakes: Treats 'one consolidated org' as a given instead of evaluating which units genuinely need to stay separate
Attempts to merge all 14 units' legacy data models and customizations wholesale
Plans a single big-bang cutover instead of staged, per-unit migrations with independent rollback plans
Doesn't use the consolidation as an opportunity to retire undocumented legacy automation
Underestimates the reconciliation/validation effort needed per business unit before cutover
keyPoints: Distinguishes genuine business-model differences from historical accidents of separate acquisition
Designs a canonical data model from actual requirements, not a merge of all legacy models
Stages migration by business unit with independent cutover and rollback plans
Uses the consolidation as a forcing function to retire undocumented legacy automation
Keeps genuinely different units separate with a thin integration layer rather than forcing consolidation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly evaluates which units should consolidate vs. stay separate
Designs a sound canonical data model approach rather than a wholesale merge

deepDive.heading: Scoping the real decision: consolidate what, and why
deepDive.content: The board's ask is cross-sell reporting and shared service, not literal oneness — so the design starts by sorting the 14 orgs into 'genuinely different' (a regulated subsidiary with distinct compliance obligations, a unit with a fundamentally different sales motion like usage-based vs. one-time sale) versus 'different by accident of acquisition history.' Only the second group is a consolidation candidate. Forcing a regulated subsidiary onto the shared platform just to hit a round number of 'one org' trades a real compliance boundary for an aesthetic goal, and is exactly the kind of decision a CTA review board would tear apart.

deepDive.heading: Canonical data model design
deepDive.content: The unified Account/Contact/Case model is derived from the actual cross-sell and shared-service requirements, not assembled by superset-merging 14 units' custom fields. Each unit's existing custom objects get mapped to the canonical model through an explicit crosswalk document, and any field that can't be cleanly mapped triggers a business conversation about whether it's still needed at all — a decade of acquired orgs reliably contains fields and processes nobody can explain anymore, and this is the only time anyone will have a mandate to clean that up.

deepDive.heading: Staged, risk-contained migration
deepDive.content: Each business unit gets its own migration wave with a dedicated data reconciliation step (record counts and key financial totals cross-checked between source and target before cutover), a rehearsed cutover window scheduled around that unit's own sales cycle quiet periods, and a defined rollback point. Waves are sequenced by risk and dependency — units with no cross-dependencies run in parallel to compress the 18-month timeline, while units sharing customers or integrations with already-migrated units run after those are stable. No unit's cutover is allowed to risk another unit's ability to close deals, which is the architectural reason for staging instead of a single cutover.

deepDive.heading: Integration layer for units that stay separate
deepDive.content: For the business units that have a genuine reason to remain on their own platform, a thin, purpose-built integration (CDC or scheduled sync into a shared reporting layer, or a Snowflake-based consolidation for cross-sell analytics) satisfies the board's actual requirement without forcing a false consolidation. This also reduces risk: a unit that stays separate can continue operating completely unaffected by the migration program running elsewhere.

deepDive.heading: Governance during the transition
deepDive.content: An 18-month program touching 14 business units needs its own lightweight architecture review cadence — not a committee that blocks every change, but a standing checkpoint before each wave's cutover to confirm the reconciliation results, rollback readiness, and integration impact are all signed off. This is also where legacy automation audit happens: anything undocumented and unowned gets flagged during that unit's migration wave rather than ported forward silently.

deepDive.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
deepDive.content: The two failure modes that kill a project like this are (1) treating consolidation as all-or-nothing, which either forces inappropriate units together or stalls the whole program waiting for consensus across 14 stakeholders, and (2) attempting a single cutover to hit the 18-month deadline faster, which maximizes blast radius exactly when the board has said no unit can afford downtime. The tradeoff the architecture explicitly accepts is a longer timeline (staged waves) in exchange for contained risk, and the explicit recommendation to the board is that 18 months is achievable for the consolidation candidates, while genuinely separate units achieve the board's actual goal (cross-sell visibility) through integration rather than forced merger.

questions.title: System Design: Identity and Security Architecture for a Regulated Multinational
questions.prompt: A multinational financial services firm operating in the US, EU, and Singapore needs a Salesforce identity and security architecture that satisfies data residency requirements per region, supports SSO through a corporate identity provider, enforces field-level encryption on financial data, and gives regulators an auditable access trail. Design the architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Data residency across US, EU, and Singapore almost certainly rules out a single global org as the starting assumption, since Salesforce orgs are provisioned in specific data center regions and genuine data residency obligations (as opposed to merely preferred data locality) typically require that regulated data for a jurisdiction physically resides in-region, which points toward either separate regional orgs or, if a single org is required for other business reasons, a very careful review of exactly which data elements have hard residency requirements versus which can live in a consolidated org with regional access controls layered on top. SSO through the corporate identity provider should use SAML or OpenID Connect federation with that IdP as the single source of truth for authentication, with Salesforce configured as a service provider validating signed assertions, and Multi-Factor Authentication enforced at the IdP level so it's consistent across every connected application, not just Salesforce — I'd avoid provisioning any local Salesforce passwords at all for regulated users, since a local credential is both an unnecessary attack surface and a second place for stale access to persist after an employee leaves. Field-level encryption via Shield Platform Encryption on financial data needs a deliberate choice between deterministic and probabilistic modes per field based on whether that field needs to support filtering/reporting, and critically, Shield's Key Management needs its own key rotation policy and a documented key-custody model, since regulators specifically ask who can access encryption keys and under what control, not just whether encryption exists. The auditable access trail requirement needs Field Audit Trail (for field-level history retention beyond standard field history tracking limits) combined with Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring (or Real-Time Event Monitoring) capturing login events, report exports, and API access at a granular level, retained and exported to a SIEM or long-term archive the regulator can actually query, because Salesforce's native retention windows for some event log data are shorter than typical multi-year regulatory audit requirements, so the architecture needs an explicit export/archive pipeline, not just native logging turned on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first architectural decision I'd force, before anything else, is whether this genuinely needs separate regional orgs or a single org with regional controls — and for a financial services firm specifically, I'd assume real data residency obligations until proven otherwise, which usually points toward regional orgs or at minimum a very deliberate review of which specific data elements actually have to stay in-region. For identity, I want the corporate IdP to be the only place authentication actually happens — SAML or OIDC federation into Salesforce as the service provider, MFA enforced at the IdP so it's consistent across every system the company uses, and no local Salesforce passwords for regulated users at all, because that's both an extra attack surface and a place stale access can linger after someone leaves. For the financial data itself, Shield Platform Encryption is the right tool, but I wouldn't just turn it on — I'd go field by field deciding deterministic versus probabilistic based on whether that field needs to support real filtering or reporting, and I'd make sure there's an actual documented key rotation and custody policy, because that's exactly the kind of thing a regulator asks about directly. And for the audit trail, native Salesforce logging alone won't cut it for a multi-year regulatory look-back — I'd pair Field Audit Trail and Event Monitoring with an explicit export pipeline into a SIEM or long-term archive, because Salesforce's own retention windows on some of that event data are shorter than what a regulator might actually ask to see.
commonMistakes: Assumes a single global org without evaluating actual data residency obligations per region
Provisions local Salesforce passwords for regulated users alongside SSO instead of eliminating them
Enables Shield encryption without a documented key rotation/custody policy
Relies on native Salesforce log retention windows without an export/archive pipeline for long-term audit
Treats encryption mode (deterministic vs. probabilistic) as a one-size-fits-all default rather than a per-field decision
keyPoints: Correctly evaluates data residency implications before assuming a single-org architecture
Designs SSO/MFA federation through the corporate IdP with no local password fallback
Makes deliberate, per-field encryption mode decisions tied to actual field usage
Documents a key rotation and custody policy for Shield Platform Encryption
Designs an explicit audit log export/archive pipeline meeting multi-year regulatory retention needs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly addresses data residency and org topology implications
Designs a sound SSO/MFA/identity federation architecture
Correctly designs field-level encryption with key management
Designs an adequate, regulator-ready audit trail architecture

deepDive.heading: Data residency and org topology
deepDive.content: Residency obligations in financial services are usually genuine, not preference, so the design starts from regional orgs (or a validated single-org exception with regional data partitioning) rather than defaulting to one global org for convenience. The architecture inventories which specific objects/fields actually carry regulated data per jurisdiction, since not everything in the org is subject to residency rules, and that inventory drives whether full regional separation or a narrower regional-data-isolation pattern is sufficient.

deepDive.heading: Identity federation and access
deepDive.content: SAML or OIDC federation makes the corporate IdP the sole authentication authority; Salesforce trusts signed assertions and never issues or validates a local password for a regulated user. MFA is enforced at the IdP layer so policy is consistent across every federated application, and session policies (timeout, IP restrictions) are set per region to reflect each jurisdiction's own security expectations, not a single global default.

deepDive.heading: Field-level encryption and key management
deepDive.content: Shield Platform Encryption is applied field-by-field: deterministic where exact-match filtering or reporting is a real requirement (with the pattern-leak tradeoff explicitly accepted by compliance), probabilistic everywhere else for maximum protection. Key rotation cadence and custody (who can initiate rotation, how key material is protected, what happens on a suspected compromise) is documented as a formal policy, since 'encryption is on' is not an answer regulators accept without a key governance story behind it.

deepDive.heading: Auditable access trail
deepDive.content: Field Audit Trail extends field-history retention beyond standard limits for the specific regulated fields; Event Monitoring (or Real-Time Event Monitoring) captures logins, report exports, and API calls at the record and field level. Because native retention windows for some event data are shorter than multi-year regulatory look-back periods, every relevant log stream is exported on a schedule into a SIEM or archive store the compliance team (and, if needed, a regulator) can query independently of Salesforce's own retention.

deepDive.heading: Cross-region integration and reporting
deepDive.content: Where cross-region visibility (a global executive dashboard, cross-border risk reporting) is a genuine business need despite regional data separation, that's satisfied through an aggregation layer — a reporting warehouse receiving permitted, possibly anonymized or aggregated extracts from each region — rather than by weakening the regional data boundary itself. This keeps the residency guarantee intact while still answering the business's real cross-region questions.

deepDive.heading: Governance and ongoing compliance
deepDive.content: The architecture includes a recurring access review (who has field-level access to encrypted financial data, reviewed on a fixed cadence, not just at go-live), a documented incident response plan specific to a key-compromise or unauthorized-access scenario, and an explicit owner for keeping the encryption/audit configuration in sync as new fields and objects are added over time — since the single most common way this kind of architecture degrades is a new field added later that nobody remembers to bring under the same encryption and audit coverage as everything else.

questions.title: Multi-Org Strategy: A Decision Framework for Split vs. Consolidate
questions.prompt: A newly-acquired business unit's leadership wants to keep operating on its own Salesforce org indefinitely, arguing their sales process is too different to merge. Corporate IT wants one org for cost and reporting reasons. As the architect asked to make the actual recommendation, what framework do you use to decide, independent of either side's preference?
questions.modelAnswer: The decision framework has to separate genuine architectural differentiators from preferences or inertia on either side: a real case for staying separate includes a materially different sales process that would require extensive customization to coexist cleanly in a shared object model (different stage definitions, different approval hierarchies, different product/pricing structures that don't map onto the parent's configuration without significant compromise), a distinct regulatory or compliance boundary, or genuinely incompatible data volumes/usage patterns that would create governor-limit or performance contention if forced to share infrastructure; a weak case for staying separate, by contrast, is 'we've always done it this way' or 'our team prefers our own system,' which are real concerns about change management, not architectural requirements. Corporate IT's cost and reporting argument is also not automatically correct just because it's the default institutional preference — the actual cost of consolidation (migration effort, retraining, risk to the acquired unit's near-term sales performance during transition) needs to be honestly weighed against the actual benefit (license consolidation savings, unified reporting), and if the acquired unit is small relative to the parent and genuinely has a different sales motion, the reporting gap can often be closed more cheaply with a lightweight integration or a shared analytics layer than with a full platform consolidation. My actual recommendation process is: document the specific, concrete differences the business unit claims (not accept 'too different' as a conclusion, get the actual field/process list), evaluate each one against whether it's a true architectural blocker or a configuration/change-management issue that a well-designed shared object model (using record types, page layouts, and process variations within one org) could actually accommodate, and present the board with the real cost/benefit of each path rather than picking a side based on which stakeholder is more senior or more persistent. In my experience the correct answer is very often a middle path — one platform with deliberate configuration flexibility for the acquired unit's genuine differences, rather than either a forced full merge or permanent separation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't let either side's preference decide this — I'd ask the business unit to actually list, specifically, what about their sales process is different, not just accept 'it's too different' as an answer, because half the time what gets called 'too different' turns out to be a few stage names and an approval step that a shared org with record types and the right page layouts could handle just fine. The things that would actually justify staying separate are a real regulatory boundary, a genuinely incompatible data volume situation, or a sales process different enough that forcing it into the parent's model would require so much compromise it's not worth it — not 'we like our own system' or 'we've always done it this way,' which are real feelings but not architectural arguments. And I'd push back on corporate IT just as hard — cost and reporting benefits are real, but so is the real cost and risk of migrating a newly acquired unit during a period when you really don't want to disrupt their ability to sell. My actual recommendation almost always ends up being a middle path: one platform, but with deliberate configuration room — record types, layouts, process variants — for whatever's genuinely different about this unit, rather than either forcing a full merge or just letting them stay separate forever because nobody wanted to have the harder conversation.

Accepts corporate IT's cost/reporting argument as automatically correct without weighing migration risk/cost
Treats this as a binary choice (fully separate vs. fully merged) instead of considering configuration flexibility within one org
Decides based on which stakeholder is more senior or persistent rather than architectural merit
Doesn't distinguish genuine architectural blockers from change-management/preference concerns
keyPoints: Requires concrete, specific evidence of differences rather than accepting a vague claim
Distinguishes true architectural blockers from configuration or change-management concerns
Honestly weighs corporate IT's consolidation benefit against real migration cost and risk
Considers a middle-path architecture (one org, deliberate configuration flexibility) as a real option
Makes the recommendation based on architectural merit, not stakeholder seniority or persistence

questions.title: Architecture Decision: Choosing Between Platform Events, CDC, and Pub/Sub API for Real-Time Inventory Sync
questions.prompt: A retail client needs near-real-time inventory level sync between an external warehouse management system and Salesforce Order Management, with the warehouse system as the source of truth. Design the event-driven integration, naming which specific technology handles which part and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the warehouse management system is the source of truth and is external to Salesforce, the inbound direction (warehouse to Salesforce) is a custom Platform Event, not Change Data Capture, because CDC only publishes change events for changes happening inside Salesforce itself — there's no Salesforce-side DML to capture for an inventory level that changed in an external system, so the warehouse system needs to actively publish an InventoryLevelChanged__e event (via the REST API's sObject Events endpoint, authenticated through a dedicated integration user) whenever a SKU's available quantity changes, with a payload carrying the SKU identifier and new quantity rather than a full record diff. On the Salesforce side, a subscriber (either a Platform Event trigger or an external subscriber using the Pub/Sub API if the consuming logic actually lives outside Salesforce, such as in a separate order-orchestration service) updates the corresponding Product/Inventory record, and this subscriber needs to be designed for high-frequency, bulk-friendly processing, since inventory changes in a real retail operation can be high volume and bursty, meaning the event payload should be designed for Platform Event's bulk publish/consume patterns rather than one event per unit of inventory movement. If any other downstream system (a separate analytics pipeline, a partner-facing API) also needs to know about Salesforce-side changes to Order or Product records themselves, that's where CDC fits — enabling CDC on the Order object so any external subscriber using the Pub/Sub API gets a reliable, platform-generated change stream of Order updates without Salesforce needing to write and maintain a custom publish-event trigger for that separate concern. I'd also design for eventual consistency explicitly rather than pretending this is synchronous: Salesforce's Order Management view of inventory should be treated as a near-real-time cache of the warehouse system's truth, with a reconciliation job (scheduled, comparing a sample or full set of SKU quantities between systems) catching any drift from a missed or failed event, because an event-driven architecture without a reconciliation safety net eventually accumulates silent drift from any dropped or failed delivery.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key distinction I'd make clear upfront is that CDC and Platform Events solve different directions of this problem, and conflating them is the most common mistake here. Since the warehouse system is external and is the source of truth, the warehouse-to-Salesforce direction has to be a custom Platform Event — CDC only fires on changes happening inside Salesforce, there's nothing for it to capture when inventory changes in an external system, so the warehouse system needs to actively publish an event with the SKU and new quantity whenever something changes. On the Salesforce side, whatever subscribes to that event and updates the Product/Inventory record needs to be built for real volume and bursts, not one-event-at-a-time thinking, because retail inventory changes can come in fast. If there's a separate direction — something else needing to know when an Order or Product record changes inside Salesforce itself — that's exactly where CDC earns its place, since it gives any external subscriber a reliable change stream with zero custom publish logic needed on our side. And I'd be upfront with the client that this is eventual consistency, not real-time truth — Salesforce's view of inventory is a near-real-time cache of what the warehouse system actually has, and I'd build in a scheduled reconciliation job to catch drift from any event that got dropped or failed to deliver, because an event pipeline with no reconciliation safety net quietly drifts out of sync over time and nobody notices until a customer orders something that's actually out of stock.

Designs the subscriber for one-event-at-a-time processing instead of high-volume, bulk-friendly handling
Presents the integration as real-time/synchronous instead of explicitly eventual consistency
Has no reconciliation mechanism to catch drift from missed or failed event deliveries
Conflates Platform Events and CDC as interchangeable rather than fitting each to the correct direction
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the warehouse-to-Salesforce direction as a custom Platform Event, not CDC
Correctly identifies CDC as fitting a separate Salesforce-to-external-system change stream need
Designs the subscriber for high-volume, bulk-friendly event processing
Explicitly frames the integration as eventual consistency with a near-real-time cache model
Includes a reconciliation mechanism to catch drift from missed/failed events

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns Platform Events vs. CDC to the right direction/use case
Designs for volume/bulk processing appropriately
Correctly frames and designs for eventual consistency
Includes a reconciliation mechanism for drift detection

questions.title: Defending a Trigger/Domain/Service/Selector Layering Decision to a Hostile Review Board
questions.prompt: In a Certified Technical Architect-style review board, a panelist aggressively challenges your choice to implement full Apex Enterprise Patterns layering (Selector/Domain/Service) for a mid-complexity org, arguing you've over-engineered a solution that didn't need it. Defend your design decision under that pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: The defense has to be grounded in the actual requirements that drove the decision, not a generic appeal to best practice, so I'd restate the specific reuse and longevity factors present in this case: if this logic is genuinely called from multiple entry points (a trigger, an invocable action used by Flow, a REST endpoint for a partner integration) and multiple developers across a multi-year roadmap will maintain it, the layering isn't decoration, it's the mechanism that prevents the same business rule from being implemented three slightly different ways across those entry points — I'd cite the specific entry points and roadmap, not assert the principle abstractly. If the panelist's challenge has actual merit — if, on reflection, this particular object really only has one entry point and a short expected lifecycle — the right response in a review board is not to defend the decision reflexively, but to acknowledge that the pattern's value is conditional and explain precisely which conditions made it the right call here, which demonstrates judgment rather than dogma; a CTA-level answer that insists every design decision was unambiguously correct regardless of pushback is itself a red flag to an experienced panel, since real architecture always involves tradeoffs a reasonable person could weigh differently. I'd also address cost directly rather than avoiding it: yes, this is more files and more initial setup than a straightforward trigger-to-handler pattern, and I'd quantify that cost honestly (additional classes, slightly longer onboarding for a new developer) against the specific, named benefit (reuse across the stated entry points, testability, avoiding duplicated business logic) rather than asserting the benefit outweighs the cost without showing the math. Finally, I'd invite the specific counter-scenario the panelist seems to be implying — ask what alternative they'd propose given the same reuse/longevity facts — because a hostile challenge in a review board is often testing whether the candidate can hold a position under pressure with evidence, not whether the candidate will fold or double down without engaging the actual substance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't get defensive here — I'd go straight back to the actual facts that drove the decision. This logic gets called from a trigger, an invocable action Flow uses, and a REST endpoint for a partner integration, and it's going to be maintained by more than one developer over a multi-year roadmap — those are the specific reasons the layering earns its cost here, not some abstract 'this is best practice' answer. If the panelist's pushback actually has a point — if this case turns out to be simpler than I thought — I'd rather say so directly than dig in just to win the argument, because insisting every decision I ever made was perfect regardless of pushback is a worse look in front of an experienced panel than showing I can reconsider with judgment. I'd also just be honest about the cost — yes, this is more files and a steeper ramp for a new developer than a plain trigger-and-handler-class approach, and I'd actually name that cost instead of pretending it doesn't exist, then weigh it against the specific reuse and maintainability benefit I already named. And if the panelist is implying there's a better alternative, I'd ask them directly what they'd propose given the same facts, because that's usually the real point of a hostile challenge like this — not whether I'll cave, but whether I can actually engage with the tradeoff instead of just repeating the conclusion louder.
commonMistakes: Responds to pushback with a generic 'best practice' appeal instead of case-specific facts
Reflexively defends the decision without engaging honestly with the cost being challenged
Refuses to acknowledge any merit in the challenge even when the challenge has a legitimate point
Doesn't quantify the actual cost (extra files, onboarding complexity) being traded off
Gets visibly rattled or defensive rather than engaging with the substance of the challenge
keyPoints: Grounds the defense in the specific reuse/longevity facts of this case, not abstract principle
Honestly acknowledges the real cost of the chosen pattern
Shows willingness to reconsider if the challenge has genuine merit, rather than dogmatic defense
Invites the panelist to propose a concrete alternative given the same facts
Maintains composure and substantive engagement under adversarial pressure

Honestly engages with and quantifies the real cost of the decision
Shows calibrated judgment rather than dogmatic defensiveness
Maintains composure and substantive engagement under pressure

questions.title: Enterprise Apex Architecture: fflib-Style Layering Tradeoffs at Scale
questions.prompt: An enterprise org with 40+ Apex developers across 6 scrum teams is standardizing on Apex Enterprise Patterns (fflib) for all new development. Design the governance around this standardization, and name the specific tradeoffs that show up at this scale that don't show up in a smaller org.
questions.modelAnswer: At 40+ developers across 6 teams, the governance challenge shifts from 'should we use this pattern' to 'how do we keep 6 teams' interpretations of the same pattern from drifting into 6 subtly different dialects of it' — without a concrete, enforced standard for exactly how Selector, Domain, and Service classes are named, structured, and allowed to depend on each other across domain boundaries, each team will reasonably but independently fill in the gaps differently, and six months later code review between teams becomes an argument about style rather than substance. The governance needs: a small number of concrete, example-backed conventions (not just 'use fflib') covering class naming, where cross-domain Service-to-Service calls are allowed versus discouraged, and how a Domain class for one object is permitted to reference another object's Domain or Selector, published as a living reference implementation other teams can literally copy rather than a prose document; a static analysis rule set (via PMD or a custom linter) that mechanically enforces the structural conventions that matter most (no SOQL outside Selector classes, for instance) rather than relying on code review alone to catch violations across 6 teams' worth of pull requests; and a cross-team architecture guild or a rotating review function that specifically reviews new Domain/Service boundaries before they're established, since the boundary decisions (what counts as one domain versus two) are exactly the design decisions most likely to diverge team-to-team without any entanglement, leading to duplicate or conflicting logic across teams that technically both followed 'the pattern' but disagree about where its edges are. The tradeoff that's genuinely different at this scale versus a small org: in a 5-developer org, inconsistency is cheap to fix because one person can review and correct it; at 40+ developers across 6 teams, inconsistency compounds because each team builds on top of what's already there, so correcting a drifted convention after 6 months means touching code owned by multiple teams, which is a coordination cost that didn't exist when there was effectively one team making every decision.
questions.professionalAnswer: At this scale, the real risk isn't that one team does Apex Enterprise Patterns badly — it's that six teams each do it reasonably, but differently, and eighteen months later you've got six dialects of the same pattern that don't actually interoperate cleanly. So the governance I'd put in place isn't just 'read this document about fflib,' it's a small set of concrete conventions with actual example code — naming, where cross-domain calls are and aren't allowed, how one object's Domain class is permitted to touch another object's data — published as a reference implementation teams can literally copy from, not prose they have to interpret. I'd also back that up with static analysis that mechanically catches the structural violations that matter most, like SOQL showing up outside a Selector class, because relying on code review alone across six teams' worth of pull requests means inconsistent enforcement no matter how good everyone's intentions are. And I'd want some kind of cross-team review specifically for new domain boundary decisions — what counts as one domain versus two — because that's the exact decision point where teams drift apart without even realizing it, each one technically 'following the pattern' while disagreeing about where it actually applies. The thing that's genuinely different here versus a small team is the cost of fixing drift later — with five developers, one person notices and fixes an inconsistency in an afternoon; with forty developers across six teams building on top of each other for months, untangling a drifted convention means touching code three other teams now depend on, and that's a real coordination cost that just doesn't exist at a smaller scale.
commonMistakes: Treats 'adopt Apex Enterprise Patterns' as sufficient governance without concrete, example-backed conventions
Relies only on code review to enforce structural conventions across 6 independent teams
Has no explicit mechanism for reviewing new domain boundary decisions before they're established
Doesn't name the specific scale-dependent cost (coordination cost of fixing drifted conventions later)
Assumes the governance needs of a 40-developer, 6-team org are the same as a 5-developer team
keyPoints: Provides concrete, example-backed conventions as a living reference, not just a stated preference
Uses static analysis to mechanically enforce key structural conventions across teams
Establishes a cross-team review mechanism for new domain boundary decisions
Names the specific scale-dependent tradeoff (coordination cost of correcting drift later)
Correctly distinguishes the governance needs of this scale from a smaller team's needs

questions.title: Designing an API Gateway / Middleware Governance Pattern Across Dozens of Integrations
questions.prompt: An enterprise has accumulated 50+ point-to-point integrations directly against Salesforce's APIs from various internal systems and partners, with no central visibility into what's calling what. Design the middleware/API gateway architecture to bring this under control, and explain what you'd do about the existing 50 integrations rather than just governing new ones.
questions.modelAnswer: The core architectural shift is from point-to-point integration (each external system calling Salesforce's REST/Bulk/SOAP APIs directly) to a hub pattern where an API gateway or integration platform (MuleSoft, given its native Salesforce ownership and purpose-built connectors, is the obvious default, though the principle applies to any capable iPaaS) sits between external systems and Salesforce, providing centralized authentication/authorization, rate limiting, request/response logging, and a stable published contract (a well-documented API or set of APIs) that external systems integrate against instead of Salesforce's raw platform APIs directly — this gives the architecture team actual visibility (every call passes through one observable layer) and a single point of control for things like deprecating an old field or object without having to track down every direct consumer individually. For the existing 50 integrations, a wholesale 'migrate everything through the gateway immediately' mandate is unrealistic and risky, so I'd inventory them first (which requires actual discovery work — connected app usage logs, API usage reports, and interviews with system owners, since 'no central visibility' means the inventory itself doesn't exist yet) and triage by risk and value: integrations that are business-critical, high-volume, or touch sensitive data get prioritized for migration to the gateway first, since those are both the highest-risk point-to-point connections and the ones where centralized control delivers the most immediate value; low-risk, low-volume, or soon-to-be-decommissioned integrations can be deprioritized or left as-is temporarily rather than spending migration effort on something that may not need to exist in a year. Governance going forward needs a hard rule enforced structurally, not just by policy: no new direct point-to-point integration against Salesforce's platform APIs gets approved without an explicit architectural exception, with the default path being integration through the gateway, and that rule needs teeth — restricting which connected apps/integration users have direct API access by default, and requiring architecture sign-off to provision a new one outside the gateway pattern, rather than relying on every team remembering a written policy.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fundamental shift I'd make is from fifty different systems calling Salesforce's raw APIs directly to one gateway sitting in the middle — MuleSoft is the obvious default given it's owned by Salesforce and has native connectors, but the principle holds with any capable integration platform. That gateway becomes the one place authentication, rate limiting, and logging actually happen, and the one place I can see everything that's calling Salesforce, which solves the 'no central visibility' problem directly. For the existing 50, I wouldn't mandate migrating all of them at once — that's unrealistic and it's also risky, moving a bunch of working integrations at the same time. First I'd actually build the inventory, because if there's no central visibility today, that inventory doesn't exist yet — connected app logs, API usage reports, conversations with whoever owns each system. Then I'd triage by risk and value: the business-critical, high-volume, sensitive-data integrations get migrated to the gateway first, because those are exactly the ones where staying point-to-point is riskiest and where centralizing control pays off fastest. The low-risk, low-volume ones I might just leave alone for now rather than spending migration effort on something that might get decommissioned anyway. And going forward, I wouldn't rely on a written policy alone to stop new point-to-point integrations from popping up — I'd restrict direct API access structurally, so provisioning a new connected app with direct platform access requires an actual architecture sign-off, making the gateway the default path by how access is actually granted, not just by what the policy document says it should be.
commonMistakes: Mandates migrating all 50 existing integrations to the gateway immediately rather than triaging by risk
Assumes an inventory of existing integrations already exists instead of treating discovery as real work
Relies on written policy alone to prevent new point-to-point integrations, with no structural enforcement
Doesn't prioritize business-critical/high-risk integrations for migration over low-risk ones
Picks a gateway/middleware technology without explaining why it fits this specific Salesforce context
keyPoints: Designs a hub-pattern gateway architecture replacing point-to-point integration
Treats inventory/discovery of existing integrations as necessary, non-trivial first work
Triages existing integrations by risk/value rather than migrating all at once
Enforces the no-new-point-to-point rule structurally (access provisioning), not just by policy
Explains why the chosen middleware approach fits the Salesforce integration context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound gateway/middleware architecture
Treats discovery/inventory of existing integrations as necessary work
Triages existing integrations by risk rather than an all-at-once migration
Enforces future governance structurally, not just by written policy

questions.title: Designing a Release and Environment Strategy for 50+ Development Teams
questions.prompt: A global enterprise with 50+ Salesforce development teams across different business units needs a sandbox and release strategy that gives each team autonomy to move fast, while preventing any one team's release from breaking another team's work in a shared production org. Design the environment and release governance architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: The environment strategy needs a tiered sandbox model where each team works in its own Developer or Developer Pro sandbox (or scratch orgs for source-driven teams) for isolated feature development, merges into a shared integration sandbox (or a small number of them, segmented by business domain rather than one single integration environment for all 50 teams, since a single shared integration sandbox for 50 teams just recreates the same contention problem one layer earlier) where cross-team conflicts surface early, then promotes through a full-copy or partial-copy UAT/staging environment that mirrors production configuration closely enough to catch issues a sandbox with sparse data wouldn't, before reaching production. The release governance layer needs a defined release train model — fixed, predictable release windows (weekly or biweekly, depending on the org's risk tolerance) that every team's changes feed into, rather than continuous, uncoordinated deploys straight to production by individual teams, because with 50 teams, uncoordinated deploys are exactly what creates the 'one team's release breaks another team's work' problem the question describes; a release train forces visibility into what's shipping together in each window, which is what lets a change-impact review happen before problems reach production instead of after. Governance also needs real teeth at the metadata-dependency level: a change-impact analysis step (either tooling-assisted, scanning for dependencies between a given release's changed components and other teams' known-owned metadata, or a lighter-weight cross-team notification requirement for changes touching shared objects) specifically for the shared metadata surfaces — standard objects, widely-used custom objects, shared Apex utility classes — that most commonly cause cross-team breakage, since most of the actual conflict risk concentrates in a relatively small set of genuinely shared components, not in each team's own domain-specific metadata. Finally, I'd assign clear ownership of shared/platform-level metadata (who owns the Account object's page layouts, who owns a shared Apex utility library) to a platform team distinct from the 50 feature teams, specifically because metadata with no clear single owner is what silently accumulates conflicting changes from multiple teams with nobody catching the conflict until it reaches production.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up as a tiered sandbox model — each team gets its own isolated sandbox or scratch org for actual feature development, then merges up into a shared integration environment, but I wouldn't make that one single integration sandbox for all fifty teams, because that just moves the contention problem one layer earlier instead of solving it — I'd segment integration environments by business domain so teams working on genuinely unrelated things aren't constantly colliding in the same shared space. Above that, a UAT or staging environment that's a real full or partial copy, close enough to production to actually catch the kind of issue a sparse sandbox never would, before anything reaches production. For the release process itself, I'd push hard against uncoordinated, continuous deploys straight to production by fifty independent teams — that's exactly the setup that produces 'my release broke your feature.' Instead I'd run fixed release trains, weekly or biweekly depending on risk tolerance, so there's an actual defined moment where everyone can see what's shipping together and a change-impact check can happen before it's live, not after. And I'd specifically focus governance effort on the shared metadata — standard objects, widely-used custom objects, shared Apex utilities — because that's where almost all the real cross-team conflict risk actually concentrates, not in each team's own corner of the org. I'd give that shared metadata to an actual platform team to own, because metadata with no single clear owner is exactly what quietly accumulates conflicting changes from five different teams until one of them finally breaks in production.
commonMistakes: Uses a single shared integration sandbox for all 50 teams instead of domain-segmented environments
Allows uncoordinated, continuous production deploys by individual teams instead of a release train model
Has no change-impact analysis step focused specifically on shared/cross-team metadata
Leaves shared platform-level metadata with no clear single owner across the 50 teams
Treats all metadata as equally risky instead of concentrating governance on genuinely shared components
keyPoints: Designs a tiered, domain-segmented sandbox/environment model
Establishes a release train model with fixed, predictable release windows
Includes a change-impact analysis step focused on shared metadata
Assigns clear platform-team ownership of shared, cross-team metadata
Correctly concentrates governance effort on genuinely shared, high-conflict-risk components

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound, domain-segmented tiered environment model
Establishes a release train model preventing uncoordinated production deploys
Designs change-impact analysis focused on genuinely shared metadata
Assigns clear ownership of shared/platform-level metadata

questions.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Integration Tradeoffs for a Customer-Facing Portal
questions.prompt: A customer-facing Experience Cloud portal needs to show real-time order status by calling an external fulfillment system. Design the integration pattern, explicitly weighing synchronous callouts against an asynchronous, event-driven approach, and justify your choice given the user-facing nature of the requirement.
questions.modelAnswer: A synchronous callout directly from the portal page's Apex controller to the external fulfillment system's API, executed while the customer is actively viewing the page, gives the most up-to-the-second accuracy but ties the page's responsiveness and reliability directly to the external system's availability and latency — if that external API is slow or briefly unavailable, the customer-facing page either hangs or errors, which is a materially worse user experience failure mode than showing a slightly-stale status, and this risk is magnified specifically because it's customer-facing, where a visible error has a direct reputational cost that an internal tool's occasional hiccup doesn't carry the same way. The asynchronous, event-driven alternative has the fulfillment system publish order status changes (via webhook into a middleware layer, or directly as an inbound Platform Event if the fulfillment system can call Salesforce's API) as they happen, with Salesforce maintaining a continuously-updated local cache of order status that the portal page queries directly with no external dependency in the page's own request path — this trades perfect real-time accuracy for consistent, fast, reliable rendering, and a brief lag between a true status change and the cached value updating (typically seconds, not minutes, for a well-designed event pipeline) is an acceptable tradeoff for almost any customer portal use case, since customers checking order status are not making split-second decisions based on sub-minute staleness. My actual recommendation is the asynchronous pattern as the primary path, specifically because the nonfunctional requirement that actually matters most here is portal reliability and responsiveness, not perfect real-time accuracy, and a customer-facing page's failure mode under the synchronous approach (visible error or hang) is strictly worse than its failure mode under the async approach (a status that's a few seconds behind truth) — I'd reserve a synchronous callout only for an explicit user-initiated 'refresh status now' action where the customer has explicitly opted into waiting for a live check, giving them control over the tradeoff rather than forcing every single page load to carry that external dependency.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest first instinct for a customer-facing page is to not let its load time or its uptime depend directly on some external fulfillment system's uptime, and that's really the whole argument for going async here. A synchronous callout gives perfect real-time accuracy, but it also means if that external API has a bad five minutes, this customer-facing page either hangs or shows an error — and for something customers are actually looking at, that failure mode is a lot worse than just showing a status that's a few seconds stale. So I'd have the fulfillment system push order status changes as they happen, into a local cache on the Salesforce side, and have the portal page just read that cache directly with zero external dependency in its own request path. That's a tradeoff — the status might lag true reality by a few seconds in a well-built pipeline — but customers checking an order status aren't making split-second decisions off of that kind of staleness, so it's an easy trade to make. The one place I would still use a synchronous callout is if the customer explicitly clicks something like 'check live status now' — at that point they've opted into waiting for a real-time check, and that's their choice to make, not something I'd force on every single page load by default.
commonMistakes: Defaults to a synchronous callout for every page load without weighing reliability impact
Doesn't recognize that a customer-facing failure mode carries higher cost than an internal tool's
Treats perfect real-time accuracy as more important than portal reliability without justification
Doesn't offer a user-initiated synchronous option for customers who genuinely want a live check
Assumes async caching introduces unacceptable staleness without reasoning about the actual lag tolerance
keyPoints: Correctly weighs reliability/responsiveness against real-time accuracy for a customer-facing surface
Designs an async, event-driven local cache pattern as the primary path
Recognizes the asymmetric cost of a visible customer-facing failure vs. a few seconds of staleness
Offers an explicit, user-initiated synchronous option as a secondary path
Justifies the choice based on which NFR actually matters most for this specific use case

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly weighs sync vs. async tradeoffs for this use case
Designs a sound async/event-driven caching pattern
Correctly reasons about the asymmetric cost of failure modes
Offers a sensible user-initiated synchronous fallback option

questions.title: Zero-Trust Security Architecture Considerations on the Salesforce Platform
questions.prompt: A CISO asks you to apply zero-trust principles to the company's Salesforce implementation, rather than relying on 'inside the corporate network equals trusted.' Translate zero-trust principles into concrete Salesforce architecture decisions.
questions.modelAnswer: Zero-trust's core principle — never trust based on network location alone, verify every access request on its own merits — translates concretely into several Salesforce decisions: first, replacing or supplementing simple IP-range-based trusted network configuration (which implicitly trusts 'anyone on the corporate VPN') with device- and context-aware access policies, using Salesforce's login flows, high-assurance session security levels, and step-up authentication (requiring re-verification via MFA for sensitive actions even within an already-authenticated session) so that being on the corporate network is a weak, non-sufficient signal rather than an implicit trust grant. Second, least-privilege access needs to be enforced far more granularly than typical profile-based defaults — this means auditing and tightening object and field-level permissions to the minimum each role genuinely needs (not the common anti-pattern of broad 'View All'/'Modify All' permission sets granted for convenience), using permission sets and permission set groups composed narrowly rather than one broad profile per department, and applying this same minimum-necessary-access principle to integration users and connected apps, which in many orgs quietly hold far broader API access than the specific integration they serve actually requires. Third, continuous verification rather than one-time login trust means leveraging Session Security Levels and policies that can force re-authentication for high-risk actions (exporting a large report, accessing an encrypted field) regardless of whether the session's initial login already passed MFA, since zero-trust explicitly rejects the idea that a single successful authentication event should grant unlimited-duration implicit trust for everything that session does afterward. Fourth, this needs to extend to the integration and API layer specifically, since zero-trust as a philosophy is often (incorrectly) applied only to human user access while leaving machine-to-machine API access on an older, more trusting model — every connected app and integration user should have a scoped OAuth flow, the narrowest viable permission set, and its own monitoring for anomalous usage patterns (a sudden spike in API calls from an integration user that's historically had steady, predictable volume is a zero-trust-relevant signal worth alerting on, not just a performance metric).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the CISO that the real translation of zero-trust into Salesforce terms is killing the idea that 'on the corporate VPN' means trusted — so instead of leaning on IP-range trusted networks as the main control, I'd bring in device and context-aware policies and step-up authentication, so sensitive actions require re-verification even inside a session that already logged in successfully. Least privilege needs to actually mean something here too — I'd audit for the common shortcut of broad View All or Modify All permission sets handed out for convenience, and move toward narrow, composed permission set groups that give each role exactly what it needs, nothing more. And I'd apply the exact same scrutiny to session behavior, not just login — Session Security Levels that can force re-authentication for a high-risk action like a big report export, because zero-trust explicitly says one successful login shouldn't be a blank check for everything that session does afterward. The piece I'd make sure doesn't get skipped, because it usually does, is applying all of this to the integration layer too — connected apps and integration users often quietly hold way more API access than the specific thing they're actually doing requires, and zero-trust gets applied to human logins while machine-to-machine access gets forgotten. I'd want every integration scoped to the narrowest access it actually needs, with its own anomaly monitoring, because a sudden spike in API calls from a usually-steady integration user is exactly the kind of signal zero-trust thinking says to watch for.
commonMistakes: Relies on IP-range trusted networks as the primary access control, treating network location as sufficient trust
Grants broad View All/Modify All permission sets for convenience instead of narrow, composed access
Treats a single successful login as sufficient trust for the entire session's duration
Applies zero-trust principles only to human user access while leaving integration/API access untouched
Has no anomaly monitoring on integration user API usage patterns
keyPoints: Replaces or supplements network-based trust with device/context-aware, step-up authentication
Enforces least-privilege access granularly via narrow permission sets, not broad defaults
Uses continuous/session-level verification rather than one-time login trust
Extends zero-trust principles explicitly to integration users and connected apps
Includes anomaly monitoring on API/integration usage as a zero-trust-relevant control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly translates zero-trust away from network-based trust
Designs granular least-privilege access enforcement
Designs continuous/session-based verification, not just login-time trust
Extends zero-trust principles to the integration/API layer

questions.title: LWC Component Architecture and Governance for a Large Enterprise Org
questions.prompt: A large org has 80+ custom LWC components built by different teams over several years, with significant duplicated logic (multiple components each implementing their own data table, their own error-toast pattern, their own date formatting) and inconsistent UX. Design the component architecture and governance to fix this going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: The architectural fix is establishing a shared base component library — a small, deliberately curated set of foundational components (a standard data table wrapper, a standard error/toast handling utility, a standard date/currency formatting utility, built either as base Lightning components wrapped with org-specific defaults or as genuinely shared LWC modules) that every new component is required to build on rather than each team re-implementing the same primitive independently, published as an actual installable/importable library (through a namespace or an unlocked package specifically for shared UI components) rather than documentation telling teams to 'be consistent.' Governance needs a concrete gate: any new LWC component proposal goes through a lightweight review checking whether it duplicates an existing shared component's functionality before being approved for development, which requires someone (a UI/component architecture owner, not necessarily a full committee) to actually have visibility into what's already built — an internal component catalog or Storybook-style registry documenting what exists and what it does, since the 80-components-with-duplicated-logic problem fundamentally stems from no one having had visibility into what already existed when each new component was built. For the existing 80 components, a wholesale rewrite is not realistic or valuable, so I'd triage by actual duplication impact: identify the handful of patterns (data table, error handling, formatting) that are duplicated the most times across the most components, and consolidate those specific patterns into the shared library first, migrating the highest-traffic or highest-maintenance-cost components to use them, while leaving lower-impact, rarely-touched components on their existing implementation unless they come up for other reasons (a bug fix, a feature request) that make migrating them incidental rather than dedicated rework. I'd also establish a lightweight design review specifically for UX consistency (shared component-level design tokens — spacing, color, typography — enforced through the shared library itself rather than left to each component's own CSS) since the 'inconsistent UX' half of this problem is really the same root cause (no shared foundation) producing a visual symptom rather than a separate problem needing a separate fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real fix here is building an actual shared component library — a data table wrapper, an error-toast utility, a date and currency formatter, built once as real importable components, not documented as 'please be consistent' and left to each team's judgment. I'd publish that as a real package teams actually build on top of, because the reason we've got eighty components with duplicated logic in the first place is that nobody building component number forty had any visibility into what components one through thirty-nine had already solved. So part of the fix is a catalog — something like an internal Storybook — so the next team building something new can actually see what exists before reinventing it, and a lightweight review gate that checks a new component proposal against that catalog before it gets built. For the existing eighty, I wouldn't try to rewrite all of them — that's not realistic and a lot of it wouldn't even be worth the effort. I'd figure out which specific patterns — data tables, error handling, formatting — are duplicated the most times across the most components, consolidate those into the shared library first, and migrate the highest-traffic components to use them. The lower-impact, rarely-touched ones I'd leave alone unless they come up for some other reason, like a bug fix, where migrating them becomes basically free. And I'd treat the inconsistent UX complaint as the same root cause wearing a different hat — shared design tokens for spacing, color, and type baked into the shared library itself usually fixes a lot of that visual inconsistency as a side effect of fixing the logic duplication, not as a separate project.
commonMistakes: Documents a 'be consistent' guideline without building an actual shared, importable component library
Attempts a wholesale rewrite of all 80 components instead of triaging by duplication impact
Has no review gate checking new component proposals against what already exists
Has no catalog/registry giving teams visibility into existing components before building new ones
Treats UX inconsistency as a separate problem rather than the same root cause's visual symptom
keyPoints: Designs a real, installable shared component library, not just documented guidelines
Establishes a review gate checking new proposals against existing shared functionality
Builds a catalog/registry giving teams visibility into what already exists
Triages the existing 80 components by duplication impact rather than attempting a full rewrite
Addresses UX inconsistency via shared design tokens in the library, treating it as the same root cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a real, importable shared component library and governance gate
Builds visibility (catalog/registry) into what already exists
Triages existing components by impact rather than a wholesale rewrite
Correctly connects UX inconsistency to the same root cause

questions.title: System Design: Integration Architecture Spanning ERP, Data Warehouse, Identity Provider, and Customer Portal
questions.prompt: A manufacturing enterprise needs Salesforce Sales Cloud to be the system of engagement while SAP remains the system of record for orders and inventory, a Snowflake warehouse serves as the analytics layer, Okta is the corporate identity provider, and a customer-facing Experience Cloud portal needs to show order status. Design the end-to-end integration architecture connecting all four systems.
